verdict.summary: nfs3svc_decode_writeargs walks the write payload with an unbounded vector index v. The dlen check counts tail->iov_len as received data, but the while loop can only traverse head remainder plus rq_pages (which back only page_len). An attacker-crafted WRITE RPC whose payload lies mostly in the tail (or otherwise beyond the pages backing page_len) passes all checks and drives v past the rq_vec array, producing out-of-bounds writes at rq_vec[v].iov_base/.iov_len and an out-of-bounds/NULL page read at rq_pages[v] in the host kernel nfsd process.

evidence.reason: Unbounded index v: the loop increments v with no comparison against ARRAY_SIZE(rq_vec) or the number of valid rq_pages entries anywhere in the code. When len exceeds head->iov_len - hdr plus the pages backing page_len, v runs past the rq_vec array, giving an out-of-bounds write of rq_vec[v].iov_base/.iov_len (and OOB/NULL read rq_pages[v] via page_address). Trigger: attacker (NFS client) frames a WRITE with count == len == e.g. 0x100000 ≤ max_blocksize, small head remainder and small page_len, and the rest of the payload in the tail kvec; the dlen check below is satisfied by tail bytes the walk can never reach.

The only length guard accepts tail->iov_len as 'received data' (dlen includes tail), but the vector walk in the while loop enumerates only the head remainder and rq_pages backing page_len — tail bytes are unreachable. This guard therefore admits messages whose payload length len is covered by head+tail while the page walk must run v past the allocated pages and the rq_vec array, enabling the out-of-bounds accesses at the loop sink.

assumptions: svc_max_payload(rqstp) can return values (e.g. up to 1MB on jumbo-capable transports) large enough to require more rq_vec entries than the transport allocates pages for; if max_blocksize were provably ≤ head+page coverage the trigger would narrow, but no such bound is stated in this code.

The head/pages/tail split of the incoming RPC message and the set of allocated rq_pages are determined by the sunrpc transport (standard semantics per discipline 3): pages back page_len, tail holds the trailing kvec; the sender controls this layout via RPC framing.
limitations: The exact declared size of rq_vec and the count of populated rq_pages are not shown in this snippet; the OOB write is established if v can exceed them, which follows from len up to max_blocksize combined with page_len/tail layout under attacker control.
If args->count > max_blocksize, len is clamped rather than rejected (lines 43-46); this changes behavior (later truncation instead of failure) but is not the primary memory-safety defect.

verdict.summary: runDOMAttributeGetter consumes no attacker-controlled data: className/attributeName are compile-time constants from generated bindings, holder is a same-process DOM wrapper, and every v8 Maybe/shape result is checked (descriptor via ToLocal+IsObject, getter via ToLocal+IsFunction, callFunction via ToLocal) with RELEASE_NOTREACHED on the failure arms. The fprintf uses a constant format string. The only unvalidated values — the return of the unshown classObjectOfPrivateScript and the empty v8::Local returned on the rethrow path — cannot have their failure instantiated by any quoted statement of this code or a trust-boundary producer, so no trigger or impact chain is provable here.

assumptions: classObjectOfPrivateScript, initializeHolderIfNeeded, rethrowExceptionInPrivateScript, and V8ScriptRunner::callFunction are project-internal callees not shown; their failure modes are assumed neither to occur nor to be exploitable, per the callee-semantics discipline.

className and attributeName are assumed to be compile-time string constants supplied by generated binding code; their content is not attacker-instantiable, which is why the fprintf %s uses and RELEASE_NOTREACHED paths are not treated as attacker-triggerable.
The generated caller of this function is assumed to handle the empty v8::Local returned on the rethrow path; that caller is not shown.
limitations: classObjectOfPrivateScript(scriptState, className) is consumed without a sentinel check before classObject->GetOwnPropertyDescriptor(...); if that unshown callee can return an empty Local, this would be a NULL dereference at line 3. Not provable from the given code.

RELEASE_NOTREACHED() on the descriptor/getter-miss arms terminates the renderer if the compiled private script ever disagrees with the generated bindings over class/attribute names; this is a controlled CHECK crash (potential DoS) requiring an internal inconsistency that an external party cannot instantiate.
On the callFunction failure path the function returns an empty v8::Local; any crash would occur in the unshown caller that consumes it, so the impact chain is not instantiated in this code.

verdict.summary: trim_spaces walks the index backwards (len--) without any 'len > 0' bound, so when the user-supplied string is empty or consists entirely of spaces, len reaches 0 and the loop condition reads str[-1] — one byte before the heap buffer (and conditionally writes str[-1] = '\0' there, continuing into negative indices). The attacker fully controls this via argv[1] (e.g. ./a.out "" or ./a.out "   "); no guard on any path prevents the out-of-bounds access.

evidence.reason: Root cause: the loop condition indexes str[len - 1] with no len > 0 bound, and the body's len-- deterministically drives len from 1 to 0 once trailing spaces are consumed. Trigger simulation: argv[1] = "" → strlen(buf2)=0 → len=0 → str[-1] is read out of bounds (before the 1-byte malloc'd buffer); if that heap byte equals ' ', str[-1]='\0' performs an out-of-bounds write and len continues to -1, scanning backwards through the heap. Mention sweep found no check, clamp, or bound on len anywhere (lines 8-11 only assign, test content, write, and decrement).

Origin of the tainted value: argv[1] is the documented user-input string (line 4) and is copied unmodified and unvalidated (only argc is checked at line 20) into buf2, which is passed to trim_spaces at line 34; empty or all-space content reaches the defective loop at line 9 unchanged.

assumptions: argv[1] is attacker-controlled content per the function's own documentation ('Given a user-input string'); the only check in main is on argc, not on the string's content or length.

The heap byte immediately preceding buf2 is not attacker-controlled in this code; therefore the conditional out-of-bounds write str[-1]='\0' (and further backward scanning) is a corruption primitive present in the loop but not deterministically instantiated — the confirmed impact is the guaranteed out-of-bounds read at index -1.
limitations: malloc return values for buf1/buf2/buf3 (lines 25-27) are never NULL-checked; strcpy(buf2, argv[1]) on a NULL buf2 would crash, but allocation failure of strlen(argv[1])+1 bytes is not attacker-inducible (argv is bounded by OS ARG_MAX) — environment-only robustness issue.
int len = strlen(str) truncates size_t to int; instantiating an overflow requires an argv[1] longer than INT_MAX/2, which OS argument-size limits make unreachable.
buf1 and buf3 are allocated and freed without use (lines 25, 27, 31, 32) — wasteful, not a security defect.

str[-1]==' ' leading to unbounded backward writes is conditional on heap-adjacent contents and was not counted as a separate primary defect; the guaranteed out-of-bounds read alone sustains the verdict.

verdict.summary: All attacker-controlled data (the SMTP command line 'line') reaches its memory sinks behind quoted, correctly-ordered guards: NULL and '<' checks on line, an e == NULL check before the in-place NUL write, a checked text_to_mailaddr return before any maddr use, a NULL-checked ':' memmove that is geometrically self-bounded within maddr->user, and a strlcpy sized from the destination buffer. The remaining anomalies (a potential NULL 'domain' deref in strlcpy, and the attacker-influenced '*args' consumed by the caller) are speculative: no trust-boundary party can instantiate them.

assumptions: text_to_mailaddr (not shown) NUL-terminates and bounds-copies into maddr->user / maddr->domain on success; per discipline 3 this unshown callee is used neither as a guard nor as a trigger source.
'line' points to a NUL-terminated string in a caller-owned writable buffer (the SMTP line reader's contract); all strchr/strlen/deref operations on it rely on this.
valid_localpart and valid_domainpart (not shown) are boolean validators whose return values are checked at every use.
maddr, args, and domain are non-NULL caller contracts; only 'line' content is attacker-controlled.
limitations: Speculative: if a caller ever passed domain == NULL, strlcpy(maddr->domain, domain, sizeof(maddr->domain)) on the empty-domain path would dereference NULL; the network peer cannot set this value (operator configuration), so the trigger is not instantiated in this code.
The '*args' output (text after '>' in the attacker's line, i.e. ESMTP parameters) is consumed by the caller, which is not shown; any misuse there is outside this code's impact chain.
The function mutates 'line' in place (writes NUL at '>'); this is by design and has no memory-safety consequence within this code.

verdict.summary: The single memory-copy sink (headerPut) is fully guarded in execution order: the attacker-controlled signature-header fields td.type and td.count are validated by strict registry-type equality and the [1, 16*1024*1024] count bound (with an exact-count constraint where the static table requires one), the producer headerGet and consumer headerPut are both sentinel-checked, and every failure path breaks to a nonzero return (fail-closed). No unguarded attacker-data path to any sink exists in this code.

assumptions: headerGet on sigh returns a td whose data/count/type are mutually consistent (standard rpm rpmtd contract; the producer is not shown) — this assumption cannot produce a trigger per discipline 3.
rpmtdFreeData resets the td (MINMEM data is not owned, no double-free/UAF); standard rpm API behavior.
xlateTags is a trusted static, sentinel-terminated translation table; xl->xtag values are registered tags so rpmTagGetTagType/rpmTagGetName cannot miss.
rasprintf handles the msg out-parameter per its contract; msg content is a fixed format string with no attacker-controlled format.
limitations: C1 (headerPut copying a data region smaller than count×typesize) would require the unshown headerGet to return an inconsistent td — not instantiable from this code; a defect there would belong to that callee, not this call site, since every field this code can check is checked.

C2: a count of 16777216 of a 16-byte type can drive a ~256 MiB allocation inside headerPut, but this is bounded by the quoted check and requires an input package of proportional size — bounded consumption, no amplification, recorded as a robustness consideration, not a vulnerability.
C4: passing msg == NULL to this function would fault in rasprintf on the error path — a caller-contract misuse at equal privilege with no attacker-controlled trigger.

verdict.summary: smacker_read_header never checks the return values of the attacker-size-scaled allocations av_malloc(smk->frames * 4) and av_malloc(smk->frames) (nor av_new_stream in the audio loop). A crafted SMK2/SMK4 header with a large frame count (up to 0xFFFFFF, requesting ~64MB+16MB) makes allocation failure realistically reachable; the NULL pointers are then written through at smk->frm_size[i] = get_le32(pb) / smk->frm_flags[i] = get_byte(pb) and dereferenced at ast[i]->index, crashing the victim's process that parses the attacker-supplied file (denial of service), while the code demonstrably performs the missing sentinel test elsewhere (if (!st), if(!st->codec->extradata)).

evidence.reason: Root cause: allocation results are consumed without any NULL sentinel check. smk->frames is attacker-controlled (get_le32, capped only at 0xFFFFFF by the check on line 32), so the attacker scales the requested allocation up to ~80MB from a tiny file; when av_malloc returns its failure sentinel NULL, the very next loop writes through the pointers.

Instantiated trigger sink: with frames >= 1 and frm_size == NULL (allocation failure sentinel, always in-domain), the first iteration executes smk->frm_size[0] = get_le32(pb), an invalid write through a NULL-derived pointer, crashing the process that parses the attacker's file. The identical unguarded write occurs at line 44 for frm_flags. No statement between line 36 and this sink tests either pointer.

Independent defect of the same class: av_new_stream returns pointer-or-NULL and its result is dereferenced immediately (ast[i]->index, then seven more uses on lines 71-79) with no NULL check anywhere in the loop, unlike the checked video stream at lines 47-49.

assumptions: The SmackerContext struct is not shown; smk->frames and smk->treesize are assumed unsigned 32-bit fields assigned from get_le32. Under a signed interpretation of frames, values 0x80000000-0xFFFFFFFF would pass the `smk->frames > 0xFFFFFF` gate as negatives, but both loops (i < smk->frames) would then skip, so no additional in-function corruption arises either way.
frm_size is assumed to be a 4-byte-element array and frm_flags a 1-byte array, matching the allocation sizes frames*4 and frames; the allocations and loop strides are internally consistent.
get_le32/get_byte/get_buffer on EOF are assumed to return 0/short counts rather than trap (old FFmpeg ByteIOContext semantics); the get_buffer short-read IS checked at line 92.
limitations: Lines 58-61: `smk->pts_inc = -smk->pts_inc;` is undefined behavior for pts_inc == INT32_MIN and `smk->pts_inc *= 100` overflows signed int for pts_inc > 21474836. The consequence is a corrupted (possibly negative/zero) timebase passed to av_reduce/av_set_pts_info, internal callees not shown; no memory sink in this code, so no vulnerability is claimed here.

If av_reduce performs a division, pts_inc == 0 (attacker-supplied) reaches line 63 unguarded, but av_reduce is a project-internal callee whose zero-denominator behavior is not shown; impact chain not instantiated.
smk->width/height are stored into the codec context without validation (lines 51-52); any misuse happens in downstream code not given.

The crashes at lines 41/44 occur at i == 0, so the observable impact is a process crash/DoS rather than a demonstrated controlled-corruption primitive; page-zero is assumed unmapped on the target platform.

verdict.summary: get_ls_result returns a string literal ("", static non-heap storage) on its pipe-failure, fork-failure, and realloc-failure paths, while main unconditionally calls free(output) on the returned pointer, producing an invalid free of non-heap memory (undefined behavior; abort or allocator-metadata corruption). Command execution itself is safe: dir_path is passed as a single execlp argument with no shell, so there is no command injection; buffer arithmetic in the read loop is correctly bounded.

evidence.reason: Unconditional free of the value returned by get_ls_result. On the error paths this value is the static string literal "" (returned at lines 20, 25, and 48), not a heap pointer, so free() operates on non-heap memory — undefined behavior / invalid free (CWE-590). Attacker-instantiable path: attacker-supplied dir_path whose `ls -l` listing exceeds available memory drives realloc (line 45) to return NULL, the function returns "" (line 48), and main frees that static pointer.

evidence.snippet: return "";  // Memory allocation error, return an empty string
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted pointer value: on the realloc-failure path the function returns a read-only static string literal instead of a heap allocation (same pattern at lines 20 and 25 for pipe/fork failure), which the caller then passes to free(). This also leaks the previously accumulated buffer.

assumptions: The environment's `ls` is the standard utility and PATH is not attacker-controlled relative to the process's own privilege; execlp("ls", ...) inherits PATH from the invoking environment, which under this code's trust model is the same party that supplies argv[1].
Directory listing content arriving on the pipe is bounded by the filesystem; an attacker with local filesystem write access can inflate it arbitrarily (basis for the realloc-failure trigger).
limitations: The invalid-free trigger requires an allocation/pipe/fork failure; on glibc, freeing a static pointer aborts the process rather than corrupting memory, and the crash occurs in the process of the same local user who supplied the input, so practical severity is low.
An attacker-supplied dir_path beginning with '-' is parsed by ls as an option (e.g. '-R'), causing functional misbehavior but no memory-safety or privilege impact.
Unbounded retention of the full `ls -l` output (read loop, lines 44-52) is the function's specified contract; recorded as amplification-adjacent, not a separate finding.
If strdup fails at line 59, printf("%s", NULL) at line 80 is technically undefined behavior but requires the same OOM precondition and is benign on common libc implementations.
Error-return paths skip waitpid, transiently leaving a zombie child until parent exit — robustness only.

verdict.summary: The switch on td.type in headerMergeLegacySigs enumerates only the valid rpm types (0..9) and has no default arm, so an attacker-influenced signature-header entry with an out-of-range type value (full 32-bit domain per the unshown headerNext producer) bypasses every td.count check and is passed unvalidated to headerPut at the call site — an attacker-derived type/count/pointer triple reaching a copy operation with no local validation on any path.

evidence.reason: Sink: headerPut receives td.type and td.count unvalidated for any td.type outside the enumerated set RPM_NULL_TYPE..RPM_I18NSTRING_TYPE, because the enclosing switch (lines 47-68) lacks a default arm. Trigger: a signature-header entry with tag in [HEADER_SIGBASE, HEADER_TAGBASE) (passes the line 42 range check), type outside 0..9 (matches no case, skips all count checks), and count up to 0xFFFFFFFF reaches this call with an unchecked attacker-derived size/type pair — a copy/insertion operation fed unvalidated attacker data at the call site.

Origin of the tainted values: headerNext (internal callee, not shown in this code) fills td.tag, td.type, td.count and td.data from sigh, the attacker-supplied signature header; per the width-domain rule td.type and td.count arrive with the full domain of their declared widths and are only narrowed by the checks in this function, which the missing default leaves incomplete for out-of-range types.

assumptions: headerPut with HEADERPUT_DEFAULT is assumed to copy/insert td data sized from td.type and td.count, consistent with the documented semantics of rpm's public headerPut API; the exact behavior for an out-of-range type is not shown and cannot be relied on in either direction.
sigh is assumed to originate from parsing an attacker-supplied package signature header, which is the sole purpose of this legacy-merge API; no statement in this code constrains its contents.
limitations: The concrete corruption primitive (oversized allocation, OOB read via type-table indexing, or rejected-by-callee) lands inside headerPut, which is not shown; the defect recorded is the absent local validation at the call site, per the call-site rule.
Passing NULL for h or sigh would crash inside headerInitIterator/headerIsEntry, but is a caller-contract crash with no corruption — recorded as robustness, not a vulnerability.

If headerPut rejects unknown types in its own dispatch (unverifiable from the given code), the impact reduces to failure of the merge rather than corruption; this cannot demote the missing validation in this code.

verdict.summary: The shown HHVM compact() wrapper contains no unguarded memory, injection, or authz sink. The only locally reachable failure mode — a NULL VarEnv returned by getOrCreateVarEnv() — is guarded by 'if (v)' before both compact() helper calls. The reservation 'PackedArray::MakeReserve(args.size() + 1)' is a capacity hint, not a copy bound, and its size_t wrap requires a SIZE_MAX-sized array no statement here can produce. All remaining logic (variable lookup, name handling, recursion via the PointerSet) executes inside an internal compact() overload that is not shown and receives only in-domain arguments (a Variant and an Array whose full declared domain a Variant/Array-taking helper must handle, plus a non-NULL VarEnv and a fresh Array). The unshown semantics of raise_disallowed_dynamic_call, getOrCreateVarEnv, MakeReserve, and the internal compact overload are recorded as assumptions per analysis discipline.

assumptions: raise_disallowed_dynamic_call() semantics are not shown; whether it throws (blocking dynamic calls) or merely records (fail-open) cannot be quoted from this code, so it is treated as neither a guard nor a trigger.

The internal overload compact(seen, v, ret, varname/args) is not shown; it receives only in-domain arguments (any Variant, any Array, non-NULL VarEnv guarded by 'if (v)', fresh Array, fresh empty PointerSet), so any defect inside it is not attributable to this call site.

PackedArray::MakeReserve and Array::attach are project-internal callees with unshown failure behavior; their returns are consumed without local sentinel checks (lines 6), but no dereference of the result occurs in the shown code.
limitations: If raise_disallowed_dynamic_call() does not terminate execution, the dynamic-call restriction fails open; however, the claimed harm (accessing an incorrect or uninitialized variable environment when compact is invoked dynamically) would occur inside the unshown getOrCreateVarEnv/VarEnv-lookup code, so no impact is instantiated in this snippet.

An args.size() == SIZE_MAX value would wrap 'args.size() + 1' to 0, but no statement in this code can produce such an array count; the reservation is a capacity hint and the array grows through its own bounds-safe insert path, so even under-wrap is not memory-unsafe.

An allocation failure (NULL) from PackedArray::MakeReserve consumed unchecked by Array::attach could propagate a null Array into the unshown helper; this requires an allocator failure not inducible by attacker input and a harmful use inside code not given.

verdict.summary: qemu_register_machine is a startup-time type registration helper whose only inputs (the QEMUMachine descriptor and its name) come from QEMU's own compile-time-constant machine definitions, not from any trust-boundary party. The conceivable defects — NULL m reaching g_strconcat, and the possibility that type_register retains ti.name past g_free(name) — have triggers that cannot be instantiated by attacker data and impact chains that depend entirely on unshown callers/callees.

DRMSource::read passes a DrmBuffer to the unshown DRM engine via mDrmManagerClient->decrypt, which can overwrite decryptedDrmBuffer.length; the code then uses that value with no local bound. In the non-AVC branch, memcpy(src, decryptedDrmBuffer.data, decryptedDrmBuffer.length) copies the callee-controlled length into the MediaBuffer heap allocation sized only by the original range_length(), yielding an attacker-influenced heap buffer overflow write; in the AVC branch, len = decryptedDrmBuffer.length redefines the read bound for data allocated with the original length, yielding out-of-bounds reads.

evidence.reason: Root cause: decryptedDrmBuffer.length is re-read here with no check that it does not exceed the destination capacity (the MediaBuffer allocation reached via src = data() + range_offset()). The field is initialized to len at line 14 but is passed by pointer into the DRM engine at lines 18-19, which can set it to any size_t value; the mention sweep over lines 14, 18-19, 28, 38, 79-81, 104, 105 finds no comparison of this length against len or (*buffer)->size(). Instantiated trigger: upstream read returns range_length()=1000 (1 KB MediaBuffer), decrypt returns NO_ERROR after setting length=0x100000, mime is non-AVC (or AVC with mWantsNALFragments), and this memcpy writes 1 MB of attacker-derived decrypted content into the 1 KB allocation — a heap out-of-bounds write (CWE-787).

Origin of the tainted value: the DRM engine callee receives &pDecryptedDrmBuffer, i.e. write access to decryptedDrmBuffer including its length field, and this code consumes the post-call value of that field (lines 38, 104, 105) with no sentinel, bound, or range check anywhere before use; per callee/width-domain rules the unvalidated use is the defect at this site's data flow.

Secondary sink of the same root cause: the post-decrypt, callee-mutated length becomes the bound for reads at decryptedDrmBuffer.data[srcOffset] (lines 42, 46, 49, 52, 55) and for the source side of the memcpy at line 95, while the allocation was sized new char[len] at line 15 from the original range_length(); an inflated length drives out-of-bounds reads past that allocation (writes remain guarded by the (*buffer)->size() check at line 81).

assumptions: memcpy copies exactly n bytes and MediaBuffer::size()/data()/range_offset()/set_range() have their standard framework semantics (size() = allocation capacity); no other behavior of the unshown mDrmManagerClient->decrypt, mOriginalMediaSource->read, or findCString callees is relied on — their unconstrained outputs are treated as attacker-data per the width-domain rule.
CHECK aborts terminate the process; the switch on mNALLengthSize is fully enumerated with a rejecting default, so mNALLengthSize cannot cause out-of-domain indexing.
limitations: range_offset() from the unshown upstream source: the AVC-branch write guard at line 81 bounds dstOffset relative to src = data() + range_offset(); a nonzero range_offset would let absolute writes reach data() + range_offset() + size(), past the allocation. Not promoted to primary because range_offset provenance and possible values are not shown and the primary heap-overflow trigger at line 104 already decides the verdict.
new char[len] with len from range_length() can throw on huge values; this is a resource/robustness concern, not a security defect here.
The memcpys at line 95 and 104 could also disclose adjacent heap data via over-read when the callee inflates length; this is folded into the same primary defect rather than reported separately.

verdict.summary: qemu_register_machine only installs statically compiled machine definitions; its sole sink g_strconcat(m->name, ...) lacks a NULL guard, but no trust-boundary party can instantiate a NULL m or m->name (no parsing/decoding path feeds m), and the worst-case consequence is a same-privilege startup crash, i.e. robustness, not a security impact. No attacker-derived sizes, indices, or offsets reach any memory or copy operation.

assumptions: type_register is a project-internal callee not shown in this code; its handling of ti.name (whether it takes ownership of the g_strconcat allocation) and of the class_data pointer is assumed per the QEMU type-registration convention and cannot be verified here.
g_strconcat is a standard GLib function that aborts on allocation failure rather than returning NULL, so its result needs no sentinel check at this use site.

The callers of qemu_register_machine are QEMU's own compiled-in machine definition tables (registration happens once at startup); the user-selectable -machine option only picks among registered entries and cannot construct or alter a QEMUMachine.
limitations: Candidate (CWE-476 shape): if a caller ever passed m == NULL or a QEMUMachine with name == NULL, line 4 g_strconcat(m->name, ...) would dereference NULL and crash at startup. The NULL check is genuinely absent (mention sweep of m: lines 1, 4, 7 only), but no attacker-reachable path in this code instantiates such a caller, and the crash is same-privilege self-inflicted robustness, not a vulnerability.

Potential one-time leak of the g_strconcat-allocated name string if the unshown type_register does not take ownership; depends entirely on unshown callee semantics and has no security impact at init time.

verdict.summary: fp48_write_bin validates the output length with exact-equality checks (32*RLC_FP_BYTES packed, 48*RLC_FP_BYTES unpacked) that precede every writer call in execution order; all writer sizes and offsets are compile-time constants whose total exactly equals the checked length, and all field indices into a are constant and in-range, so no attacker-controlled value can cause out-of-bounds access. The computed packed copy t is unused by the writers, but that has no memory-safety consequence in this code.

assumptions: RLC_TRY/RLC_THROW implement an exception mechanism that aborts the try block before subsequent statements (the code's own pattern — check, then RLC_THROW(ERR_NO_BUFFER), then writes — documents this intent); internal macro definitions are not shown.

fp48_new/fp8_write_bin/fp24_write_bin/fp48_pck are project-internal callees not shown; their allocation/write behavior is assumed per RELIC conventions. All arguments this code passes them are fixed constants or in-bounds sub-objects of a, so no unvalidated attacker-derived size/offset/index crosses any call site.

bin is assumed non-NULL and to address at least len bytes — a caller contract; the code itself does not document or check it, but a NULL bin yields only an equal-privilege crash of the caller's own process (robustness, not a vulnerability).
limitations: The pack branch calls fp48_pck(t, a) but then serializes the raw components of a (a[0][1], a[0][2], a[1][0], a[1][2]) instead of t. If the packed representation differs from the raw components, pack-mode serialization will not round-trip through the (not shown) fp48_read_bin/fp48_upk. This is a potential correctness bug whose security impact depends entirely on unshown reader code, so it is not scored as a vulnerability here.

The snippet is truncated: no RLC_CATCH_ANY / RLC_FINALLY { fp48_free(t); } and no function-closing brace appear, so the apparent leak of t cannot be attributed to the given code and also depends on unshown fp48_new allocation semantics.
A NULL bin parameter would crash the caller's process at equal privilege with no corruption or bypass — a robustness issue only.

verdict.summary: op_format's buffer/state mutations are each covered by a guard that is present and correctly positioned in execution order: the u_save failure sentinel is checked before any formatting occurs, the cursor line increment is bounded by 'curwin->w_cursor.lnum < curbuf->b_ml.ml_line_count', and the restored cursor is re-clamped by check_cursor(). The remaining candidates (linenr_T +1/-1 wrap at LONG extremes in the u_save arguments, and the unclamped w_old_cursor_lnum/w_old_visual_lnum delta adjustment) depend on values no statement in this code produces and on consumers not shown, so their impact chains are not instantiated in this code.

assumptions: oap fields (start/end lnum, line_count, cursor_start, is_VIsual, end_adjusted) are filled by Vim's operator machinery (do_pending_operator in normal.c), which is not shown; this code is not itself a trust-boundary intake point, as its caller chain is the interactive editor user operating at their own privilege.

format_lines, beginline, check_cursor, msgmore, u_save, redraw_curbuf_later are project-internal callees not shown; their internal validation could not be quoted and was not relied upon in either direction.
saved_cursor and cmdmod.cmod_flags are globals maintained by sibling code; saved_cursor is however written by this function before every read on the keep_cursor path.
limitations: The u_save arguments use oap->start.lnum - 1 and oap->end.lnum + 1 with no local bound; a wrap requires lnum at LONG_MIN/LONG_MAX, which no statement in this code produces and whose harmful consequence would materialize inside the not-shown u_save callee — trigger speculative.

wp->w_old_cursor_lnum / w_old_visual_lnum are adjusted by the unclamped line-count delta old_line_count with no local bound; within this code they are only written, and their redraw consumers are not shown, so no memory-safety impact is provable here.

No cross-trust-boundary attacker is identifiable for this function (it formats text on an explicit user-typed operator command), which limits the applicable threat model; if the surrounding Vim build exposes these operators via untrusted automation (e.g., modeline-triggered mappings), the analysis would need to be redone with that producer shown.

verdict.summary: gen_mtsr extracts the segment-register number SR(ctx->opcode) directly from the guest-controlled instruction word and passes it unvalidated as an index to gen_helper_store_sr. No statement in this code bounds, masks, or rejects the value; the 5-bit ISA field can carry 16-31, past the 16-entry segment-register file, so a guest (supervisor) can induce an out-of-bounds write of guest-GPR data inside the host emulator process. The missing guard is a range check such as 'if (SR(ctx->opcode) > 15) { gen_invalid(ctx); return; }' before the helper call.

evidence.reason: The SR number is taken verbatim from the guest instruction word (SR(ctx->opcode), full attacker-controlled domain, no mask/check quoted anywhere in this code) and passed as the segment-register index into the store helper at the call site. A guest executing an mtsr word with the SR field set to 16..31 (e.g. opcode 0x7F0001A4 gives SR=16) reaches the helper with an out-of-range index, producing an out-of-bounds write of guest-GPR data past the 16-entry SR array inside the host process; the mention sweep over lines 7-10 shows no bounds check, clamp, or mask on any path.

assumptions: The extraction macros SR() and rS(), the privilege macros CHK_SV/GEN_PRIV, gen_helper_store_sr, the decode/registration layer, and the segment-register array size are not shown in the given code; per the analysis rules none of them can serve as a guard, and the safety of this function is assumed to rest on them rather than on any statement shown.
The 16-entry size of the PowerPC segment-register file and the 5-bit width of the mtsr SR field follow from the ISA definition of the instruction this helper translates, not from the given code.
limitations: The rS(ctx->opcode) index into cpu_gpr is likewise unquoted in this code; architecturally the 5-bit rS field matches the 32-entry GPR file, so it was not treated as a separate primary defect.

In the full upstream source this function is registered via a decode entry whose invalid-opcode mask rejects the high bit of the SR field, constraining SR to 0-15; that enforcement is outside the given code and therefore cannot be credited here.
The actual out-of-bounds store occurs inside gen_helper_store_sr, whose implementation is not shown; the defect is recorded at the call site that passes the raw attacker-derived index.

verdict.summary: op_format contains no unguarded direct memory, copy, indexing, or injection sink. The callee failure sentinel is checked (u_save == FAIL returns before any use), the cursor-line increment is bounds-guarded (w_cursor.lnum < ml_line_count), and the saved_cursor read is covered by the same keep_cursor flag's earlier write. Candidates involving out-of-range oap->start.lnum/end.lnum/line_count/cursor_start fail on both trigger instantiation (fields are produced only by the operator's own editor command machinery at equal privilege, not by any discipline-4 trust-boundary party) and impact chain (any out-of-bounds consequence would occur inside unshown internal callees u_save/format_lines/beginline).

assumptions: oap->start.lnum, oap->end.lnum, oap->line_count and oap->cursor_start are produced by Vim's operator-dispatch code (do_pending_operator), which is not shown; this analysis assumes that machinery maintains cursor-derived line numbers within buffer bounds and initializes cursor_start before dispatch, but no statement in the given code documents or enforces this.

u_save, format_lines, beginline, msgmore, and redraw_curbuf_later are project-internal callees whose internal bounds handling is not shown; per discipline 3 their behavior can neither trigger nor protect any sink in this snippet.
curbuf, curwin, cmdmod.cmod_flags, saved_cursor, and the per-window w_old_* fields are editor-maintained globals; their producers are not shown.
limitations: C1 (speculative): if a caller ever dispatched op_format with oap->start.lnum == 0 or oap->end.lnum at LONG_MAX, the expressions oap->start.lnum - 1 and oap->end.lnum + 1 would underflow/overflow before being passed to u_save; not instantiable by any trust-boundary party in this code, and any memory-safety consequence would occur inside the unshown u_save. Would warrant a defensive clamp at the call site in the dispatching code.

C2 (speculative): a negative or huge oap->line_count passed to format_lines would be consumed inside that unshown function; no local validation exists here, but neither the trigger value nor the impact is instantiable within the given code.

C3 (speculative): curwin->w_cursor = oap->cursor_start copies a position whose validity (initialization, in-range lnum) is established only by the not-shown producer; a garbage value would first cause harm inside beginline or later redraw code, not in this snippet.

The wp->w_old_cursor_lnum/w_old_visual_lnum adjustments can drift to values outside the buffer range after large insert/delete deltas; these are redraw bookkeeping longs, consumed (with != 0 and > tests) by redraw code not shown, so no memory-safety consequence is demonstrable here.

verdict.summary: The calloc wrapper correctly guards the size_t multiplication at both allocation sinks: `if (lb && n > GC_SIZE_MAX / lb) return NULL;` executes before both `GC_malloc_uncollectable(n*lb)` and `REDIRECT_MALLOC(n*lb)`, and the floor-division comparison admits exactly the set of (n, lb) with n*lb <= GC_SIZE_MAX, blocking one-past-limit products while admitting the exact limit. The `lb &&` short-circuit also prevents division by zero, and lb==0 yields a zero-sized product at the sinks, which is in-domain.

assumptions: GC_SIZE_MAX is at most SIZE_MAX (the maximum of size_t); if it were smaller the guard would only be stricter, never weaker.
REDIRECT_MALLOC is the underlying malloc-like allocator whose NULL return is a standard, documented failure sentinel for calloc; its result is only propagated, never dereferenced in this code.
GC_init_lib_bounds() side-effect semantics (populating GC_libpthread_start/_end and GC_libld_start/_end) are internal and not shown; no memory or index sink in this code consumes its return value.
limitations: The return value of GC_init_lib_bounds() is not checked before reading GC_libpthread_start/_end and GC_libld_start/_end; if those globals remained unset (e.g., zero) the caller-range test would simply be false, causing a fall-through to REDIRECT_MALLOC — no memory-safety impact in this code.
A NULL return from REDIRECT_MALLOC on huge (but non-overflowing) allocation requests propagates as calloc returning NULL, which is standards-conforming, not a vulnerability.

verdict.summary: The code is a correct strdup implementation: the heap buffer is allocated with malloc(strlen(str) + 1), which exactly matches the number of bytes strcpy writes (content plus NUL), both str and the malloc result are NULL-checked before use, and the output is NUL-terminated. No guard is missing.

assumptions: malloc/strcpy/strlen/printf/free semantics are per the standard library (discipline 3).
argv[1] is treated as attacker-controlled content; its safety at the strcpy sink rests solely on the quoted allocation-size and NULL-check statements in this code, both of which are present.
limitations: malloc and free are used in my_strdup before '#include <stdlib.h>' appears in the file; under a compilation mode that permits implicit declarations with int-width returns (pre-C99 semantics on a 64-bit target) the (char *) cast could truncate a pointer. Modern compilers reject implicit declarations, and this is a compilation-mode artifact rather than a data-flow defect in any executed statement.
Theoretical strlen(str) + 1 overflow would require a contiguous string of SIZE_MAX bytes, which is not instantiable; recorded per STEP 4 exclusion (c).

verdict.summary: encrypted_pass can be NULL when dereferenced at 'if (encrypted_pass[0] == 0)': the only NULL check (the getspnam guard) runs before 'encrypted_pass = spwd->sp_pwdp' reassigns the pointer, and on builds without HAVE_GETSPNAM there is no NULL check at all after 'encrypted_pass = pwd->pw_passwd'. A remote RADIUS peer choosing a User-Name whose account record has a NULL password field crashes the daemon (denial of service of the network-facing authentication service).

evidence.reason: NULL pointer dereference sink. encrypted_pass is dereferenced without any NULL check on any path reaching this line: the sole NULL test (line 59) precedes the reassignment at line 63 and is absent on non-shadow builds where line 46 ('encrypted_pass = pwd->pw_passwd') is the last assignment. Attacker-instantiated trigger: an Access-Request User-Name selecting an account whose password field is NULL causes a crash of the long-running RADIUS daemon.

Taint origin defeating the only partial guard: line 59 checks 'encrypted_pass == NULL', but this assignment inside the guarded branch replaces encrypted_pass with the unchecked getspnam field spwd->sp_pwdp, which can be NULL; on builds without HAVE_GETSPNAM the origin is line 46 ('encrypted_pass = pwd->pw_passwd'), also unchecked.

assumptions: getpwnam/getspnam/getprpwnam are standard libc/NSS lookups whose returned struct fields (pw_passwd, sp_pwdp, fd_encrypt) are not narrowed by any statement in this code; NULL is treated as in-domain for these char* fields per the width-domain rule.
request->username->vp_strvalue is assumed NUL-terminated by the RADIUS decode layer (unquoted contract, but it feeds only lookup keys, not the defect).
limitations: OSFC2 build: 'if (pr_pw->uflg.fg_lock!=1)' appears to test the flag-validity field rather than the actual lock field fd_lock, which could let locked accounts pass; the semantics of struct pr_passwd are an unquoted external contract and OSFC2 is an exotic compile path, so this could not be confirmed.

Empty-password accounts return RLM_MODULE_NOOP (the code's own FIXME notes 'Maybe add Auth-Type := Accept?'); whether NOOP leads to unauthenticated access depends on the module return handling not shown, so no fail-open verdict was drawn.

The trigger requires an account record whose password field is NULL (malformed/NIS-sourced entry or platform where the NSS backend yields NULL); the crash is a denial of service only — no memory corruption path was instantiated.
pairmove/pairfree usage at lines 143-144 relies on internal FreeRADIUS callee semantics not shown; potential double-free/lifetime issues could not be verified from the given code.

verdict.summary: The single attacker-data input, the setting name string, is only ever used in std::string::compare (safe: pos=0 never exceeds size() and the count is clamped by the standard), exact-equality comparisons, and a log insertion reachable only for the two fixed values 'mg_name'/'mg_flags', so no memory-safety, injection, or instantiation defect exists in this code. The security enforcement for 'secure.*' settings is delegated to the not-shown ScriptApiSecurity::isSecure, whose semantics cannot be verified from the given code and thus cannot establish a fail-open trigger.

assumptions: ScriptApiSecurity::isSecure(L) is a project-internal callee not shown in this code; its return polarity (whether 'secure' denotes a sandboxed/untrusted environment, as in upstream Minetest, or a trusted one) cannot be established from the given text, so the correctness of the check 'if (ScriptApiSecurity::isSecure(L) && name.compare(0, 7, "secure.") == 0)' is neither provable nor disprovable here.

ModApiBase::getGuiEngine and script_get_backtrace are unshown callees; their returns are only NULL-tested (getGuiEngine) or streamed as data (backtrace) and are never used for memory indexing or sizing.
limitations: Candidate (speculative, not a finding): if ScriptApiSecurity::isSecure(L) returned false for untrusted mod environments, the condition on line 3 would be inverted and untrusted scripts could set 'secure.*' settings (authz bypass). This trigger requires semantics of a callee not shown in this code and therefore could not be instantiated per the analysis rules.
Log forging at the errorstream insertion on line 12 is impossible because that statement is reachable only when name is exactly 'mg_name' or 'mg_flags' (line 11 equality gate).

verdict.summary: The HTML-escaping logic is internally consistent: the sizing pass and the emit pass use identical per-character length increments ('&'→5, '<'→4, '>'→4, '"'→6, '\''→6, default→1), the buffer is allocated as malloc(len+1) from the same accumulator the writes consume, and get_welcome_message allocates total_length = strlen(prefix)+strlen(escaped)+strlen(suffix)+1, which exactly equals the bytes written by the subsequent strcpy/strcat sequence. All allocation and callee sentinel checks (escaped, message, html_escape return) precede first use. No unguarded attacker-data sink exists; remaining candidates (SIZE_MAX-scale length overflow, CWE-676 use of strcpy/strcat) are not instantiable or not defects here.

assumptions: main is the entry point and argv[1] is the attacker-influenced username; it is NULL-terminated per C runtime contract.
html_escape is only called via get_welcome_message with a checked non-NULL string; it is also a public function and was independently analyzed with its own NULL check.
limitations: Integer overflow of len or total_length would require an input string on the order of SIZE_MAX bytes, which cannot be instantiated from argv or any realistic producer; recorded as speculative.

strcpy/strcat are used, but the buffer is allocated from the identical length expressions the copies consume, so no overflow is reachable; use of these functions is therefore not a defect in this code.
printf("%s", message) outputs HTML-escaped content into a program that does not itself render HTML; no injection sink exists in the given code.

verdict.summary: Mach-O chained-fixup iterator with file-derived (attacker-controlled) segment and fixup data. Every memory sink is guarded by a quoted, correctly-ordered check: segment indexing is double-bounded (i < nsegs && i < segs_count), chained_starts entries are NULL-checked, page_size is clamped to 4096 when < 1 (prevents division by zero), page_idx is checked against page_count with the correct >= operator before the page_start[page_idx] read, page_start is NULL-checked before use, and the 8-byte file read is bounds-safe via r_buf_read_at with a != 8 sentinel check. Unsigned edge cases (limit_end - 8 underflow for limit_end < 8, start + filesize wrap producing a huge page_end_idx) were simulated and are neutralized by the while-loop gates and the page_count break; the loop is progress-guaranteed (delta != 0 break) and bounded by the read sentinel. The only unguarded use — the bin->chained_starts array pointer itself is never NULL-checked — depends on parser/caller state not shown in this code and would at most be a same-privilege crash, recorded as a limitation.

assumptions: The page_start array is allocated with page_count entries by the not-shown chained-fixup parser (same-struct invariant from the dyld chained_starts format); the quoted guard 'if (page_idx >= bin->chained_starts[i]->page_count)' is sound only under this invariant.
The segs array has segs_count entries and the chained_starts array has nsegs entries; the double bound i < nsegs && i < segs_count keeps i in-domain for both under either mapping.
r_buf_read_at clamps reads to the buffer extent and returns the byte count or -1 (standard r2 semantics); r_read_le64 reads exactly 8 bytes little-endian.
IS_PTR_AUTH/IS_PTR_BIND and the dyld_chained_ptr_* bitfield widths are the standard dyld definitions; bitfield 'next' fields are narrow (<= ~2^18-2^26 bits), so delta * stride cannot wrap ut64.
Callers of this internal iterator pass limit ranges and event masks from r2's own bin logic and gate invocation on the presence of chained fixups; this could not be verified from the given code.
limitations: bin->chained_starts (the array pointer itself) is never NULL-checked in this code; if a Mach-O with segments but no chained-fixups data could reach this function with the array unallocated, bin->chained_starts[i] would be a near-NULL read. The trigger depends entirely on the unshown parser and callers, and the impact would be a crash of the parser process at equal privilege — speculative robustness issue, not instantiated here.

'cursor <= limit_end - 8' underflows when limit_end < 8, but the enclosing while (cursor < limit_end && cursor < end) and the r_buf_read_at != 8 sentinel make the wrapped comparison unreachable/inconsequential; no memory-safety effect.

end = start + bin->segs[i].filesize can wrap ut64, producing a huge page_end_idx and a wrapped small end; the page_count break and the cursor < end gate confine the effect to skipping iteration — no out-of-bounds access.

The 8-byte read at cursor may span up to 7 bytes past the segment's end when cursor is within [end-7, end); r_buf_read_at clamps this, so at worst fixup words are parsed from adjacent file bytes (parser confusion, not memory corruption).

verdict.summary: No locally instantiable vulnerability found. All index sinks (&fdata[fx], rpmfsGetAction, setFileState) are protected against the in-code-reachable failure sentinels by the quoted guards '(fx = rpmfiNext(fi)) >= 0' and 'if (!rc && fx < 0 && fx != RPMERR_ITER_END) rc = fx;'; the free loop bound 'i < fc' exactly matches the xcalloc(fc, ...) allocation; the ensureDir sentinel '-1' is checked before first use; the failed-install erase path is deliberately rc-independent to run post hooks. The only unguarded surfaces (upper bound of fx against fc, non-NULL failedFile) require an unshown internal callee or the internal caller to violate contracts this code itself establishes, which is not an attacker-instantiable trigger.

assumptions: rpmfiNext on an iterator created in this code from 'files' returns a valid index into that file set or a negative sentinel; fc = rpmfilesFC(files) is the size of the same set, so indices are within [0, fc). Both derive from one object created/queried in this function; the negative sentinels are handled locally.
xcalloc performs overflow checking and aborts on allocation failure (rpm x-allocator semantics); xcalloc(0, ...) yields a safely freeable pointer.
The internal caller (rpmpsm) passes a non-NULL failedFile pointer; *failedFile is a write-only output parameter.
fsmMkfile takes ownership of firstlinkfile and closes it when a hardlink set completes on the success path.
fsmCommit(&fp->fpath, ...) may replace fp->fpath; each entry's pointer is freed exactly once in the exit loop.
limitations: Speculative: no local check enforces fx < fc at &fdata[fx]; an out-of-range index from the archive reader (rpmfiNewArchiveReader) or file iterator would cause OOB access (CWE-125/787). Trigger not instantiable because it requires an unshown internal iterator, constructed in this code from the same 'files' object that defines fc, to return an index outside that object — an assumption discipline 3 forbids using to produce a trigger.
*failedFile is dereferenced without a NULL check; trigger requires the not-shown internal caller to pass NULL (interface contract, not attacker data).
On a failed transaction, firstlinkfile may leak an FD if the install aborts mid-hardlink-set; the close is delegated to the not-shown fsmMkfile. Resource leak on an error path, no corruption.

TOCTOU between fsmVerify/fsmStat and the subsequent create/rename steps (plus symlink/device-node creation with package-specified targets and st_rdev) is mitigated in the not-shown fsm helpers (O_NOFOLLOW-style hardening, temp-suffix-then-rename visible via fp->suffix = tid); impact chain not characterizable from the given code.

verdict.summary: decrypt_response parses the response header (in[0], in[2], in[3], in[4]) before any check that inlen is large enough; the only length validation (line 37) runs after these reads and never establishes a minimum input length, so a malicious smart card returning a short (0-4 byte) response causes an out-of-bounds read of up to 5 bytes past the valid input.

evidence.reason: First dereference of the card-controlled response buffer with no check that inlen >= 1; if inlen == 0, this read is out of bounds. The only inlen check in the function (line 37) executes after this point and tests only the upper bound of cipher_len, not a minimum response length.

Header parsing reads in[2] (and in[3] at line 24, in[4] at line 28) with no validation that inlen covers the 3-5 header bytes; with a short attacker-controlled response (e.g. inlen = 2, in[0] != 0x99) this reads up to 4 bytes past the valid input. Mention sweep confirms inlen appears only in the line-37 check, which runs after these reads and provides no minimum-length guard, so the trigger is fully instantiated.

assumptions: The caller passes a buffer of at least inlen valid bytes (unquoted contract; not used to demote any candidate).

aes128_decrypt_cbc / des3_decrypt_cbc are project-internal helpers not shown; their block-rounding behavior for the non-block-multiple length cipher_len - 1 is unknown and was not used to trigger or to protect any sink.
exdata->smtype and exdata->sk_enc are driver-internal state set elsewhere; assumed consistent for cipher selection only.
limitations: memcpy(out, plaintext, cipher_len - 2) (line 53) copies a card-controlled length (1..4094) into a destination whose capacity is not a parameter and is not checked anywhere in this code (CWE-131 style missing size tracking); however, whether this write actually overflows depends on unshown caller buffer sizes, so the out-of-bounds-write impact is not instantiated in this code and the finding stays a design concern.
if (in[0] == 0x99) return 0; returns success without setting *out_len, potentially leaving a stale/uninitialized length for the caller; consumer behavior is not shown.
Error paths return -1 instead of SC_* error codes; functional inconsistency only.

The out-of-bounds header read is bounded to at most 5 bytes and the OOB-derived values cannot pass the line-37 check (i+cipher_len >= 5 > inlen < 5), so the read cannot be chained into a further out-of-bounds access within this function; actual disclosure/crash depends on the caller's buffer allocation.

verdict.summary: dbcs_ptr2len dereferences p[1] only under the short-circuited guard `len == 2`, which matches the table's declaration that *p is a DBCS lead byte needing a second byte; no unguarded memory access or attacker-triggerable memory-safety defect exists in this snippet.

assumptions: MB_BYTE2LEN(*p) is a table lookup whose value is in {0,1,2} per the upstream Vim byte2len table; its exact range is not shown in this code.
Callers of dbcs_ptr2len pass a pointer into a valid, NUL-terminated string; the caller's handling of a returned len of 0 or 2 is not shown in this code.
limitations: p == NULL causes a crash at `MB_BYTE2LEN(*p)` with no NULL check in this code; trigger requires a caller contract violation not producible by a trust-boundary party through this code, and the impact is a same-privilege crash with no corruption, disclosure, bypass, or amplification (robustness only).
A returned len of 0 for NUL/invalid lead bytes could be misused by callers (loop bounds, pointer advance); that use site is not given, so no impact chain is instantiated here.

verdict.summary: compand_drain indexes the delay buffer with dindex = s->delay_index without any local bound check before the first read; delay_index is persistent filter state whose producer is not shown in this code, so its full int domain is instantiable, and the only wrap (MOD at line 25) executes after the first use and cannot repair an out-of-range or negative start, yielding a heap out-of-bounds read whose value is multiplied into the output frame.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds read: dbuf[dindex] is dereferenced with dindex taken directly from persistent state (s->delay_index) with no bound, NULL, or range check on any path before this first use; the MOD wrap on line 25 runs after the read and only decrements once per step, so an out-of-domain (e.g., 100000 with delay_samples=4096, or negative) delay_index stays out of bounds for every iteration, crashing the process and leaking a clipped version of out-of-bounds memory into the output audio.

Origin of the tainted index: s->delay_index is a struct field whose producer is not shown in this code; per the width-domain rule its surface is the full int domain, and this assignment hands it unvalidated to the dbuf[dindex] read on line 23.

assumptions: The MOD macro definition is not shown in this snippet; it is assumed to be the upstream single conditional subtraction (((a) >= (b)) ? (a) - (b) : (a)), which cannot repair an out-of-range or negative start value.
s->delay_frame, s->channels[], s->delay_samples and s->delay_count are assumed to be allocated/maintained by config_output and the frame-processing path of the same filter, which are not shown.
ff_get_audio_buffer is relied on per discipline 3: it returns NULL on failure (checked here) and allocates exactly nb_samples, which makes the dst[i] write side and the delay_count subtraction safe.
limitations: Secondary candidates of the same missing-local-validation class: line 18 dereferences s->delay_frame with no NULL check and line 20 indexes s->channels[chan] with outlink->channels, neither cross-checked against allocation-time channel counts; their triggers additionally require an allocation-time mismatch in code not shown.

The concrete out-of-range delay_index value requires the unshown producer (initialization or reconfiguration) to leave it outside [0, delay_samples); under this code-only analysis that is sanctioned by the width-domain rule, but no in-code statement produces it.
Signed overflow of dindex + 1 (line 25) when dindex == INT_MAX is folded into the primary OOB-read candidate rather than reported separately.

verdict.summary: get_welcome_message documents that its output is rendered in an HTML page after login and comments claim the username is escaped, but 'escaping' is the identity assignment `char* escaped_username = username;`. The raw attacker-controlled username is concatenated verbatim (strcat) into the returned message, so markup like <script>...</script> in the username is rendered as markup — an HTML injection / XSS in the victim's post-login page. Buffer sizing itself is correct; the defect is the missing output encoding at the trust boundary.

evidence.reason: Despite the preceding comment '// Escape the username to prevent HTML injection', this is an identity assignment: no HTML encoding of the attacker-controlled username occurs anywhere in the function. The raw username flows unmodified into the message returned for HTML rendering (per the docstring), enabling HTML injection (e.g. username = '<script>alert(1)</script>') in the user's post-login page.

Sink: the unescaped, fully attacker-controlled username is concatenated verbatim into the welcome message that the code's own documentation states is rendered in an HTML page after login. No escaping, sanitizing, or rejection statement exists on any path (mention sweep covered all mentions of username/escaped_username: NULL checks only).

assumptions: The return value is consumed by an HTML renderer, as stated verbatim in the code's own docstring ('This message will be redendered in a HTML page after the user logs in'); this quoted statement is the impact link for the XSS.
The username originates outside this code (function parameter / argv[1]); its full domain is any NUL-terminated string, per the width-domain rule.
limitations: Line 23's NULL check is dead (username already checked at line 17) and line 22 assigns a const char* to a char*; both are code-quality issues with no security effect since escaped_username is never written through.

Buffer arithmetic is correct: total_length (line 32) exactly covers strcpy(prefix)+strcat(escaped)+strcat(suffix)+terminator; the only frees are commented out, so no leak/UAF in the shown flow; integer overflow would require a near-SIZE_MAX-length string, not instantiable.

verdict.summary: ff_h264_pred_weight_table iterates i over ref_count[list] (line 26) without validating ref_count against the fixed-size H264PredWeightTable arrays, then in the PICT_FRAME path writes pwt->luma_weight/chroma_weight at indices 16+2*i and 16+2*i+1; for any ref_count[list] > 8 (spec permits up to 32, and the parameter's full int domain is otherwise unconstrained) these indices reach 32..79, producing attacker-influenced out-of-bounds writes while parsing an untrusted H.264 slice header.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds write: i is bounded only by the unvalidated attacker-derived ref_count[list]; with ref_count[list] > 8 (attacker sets num_ref_idx_active in the slice header; any int is in the parameter's width domain) the indices 16+2*i and 16+2*i+1 reach 32..79, past the 32-entry first dimension of luma_weight, writing attacker-chosen values in [-128,127] (or luma_def) into adjacent decoder memory. Lines 71, 73, 74 mirror the same OOB write for luma [1] and chroma planes.

Origin of the tainted index: ref_count (const int *, attacker-controlled reference counts parsed from the slice header; producer not shown in this code) is consumed as the sole loop bound with no bounds check, clamp, mask, or error arm anywhere in the function, so i ranges over the full attacker-chosen count and flows into every array write at lines 30-31, 49-50, and 70-74.

assumptions: H264PredWeightTable's weight arrays are declared with a first dimension of 32 (luma_weight[32][2][2], chroma_weight[32][2][2][2]) per the FFmpeg header not included in the snippet; the 16+2*i overflow argument relies on this, but the width-domain trigger (ref_count[list] arbitrarily large, e.g. 2^30, making even the line-30 pwt->luma_weight[i] write OOB) stands without it.
get_ue_golomb/get_se_golomb/get_bits1 are the standard FFmpeg golomb decoders over the attacker-supplied bitstream; their returns are treated as attacker-data of int range.
limitations: Minor uninitialized reads (CWE-457/CWE-908): line 17 reads pwt->chroma_log2_weight_denom uninitialized when sps->chroma_format_idc == 0 (line 11-12 skipped its initialization), but the >7U check at line 17 clamps it to [0,7] before the shift at line 22, so no unbounded value escapes.

Lines 73-74 read pwt->chroma_weight[i][list][j] uninitialized when chroma_format_idc == 0 because the PICT_FRAME block (lines 69-76) sits outside the 'if (sps->chroma_format_idc)' guard at line 44; these reads feed the same (already OOB) duplication writes and were folded into the primary finding rather than reported separately.

The (int8_t) range checks at lines 32-33/51-52 correctly constrain stored weight values to [-128,127] (edge-tested at -128, 127, 128, and truncated inputs), so no unbounded value is written; the defect is the index, not the stored value.

verdict.summary: my_strdup allocates strlen(str) bytes, omitting the NUL terminator, then strcpy writes strlen(str)+1 bytes — a 1-byte heap out-of-bounds write on every call, including via main's attacker-supplied argv[1].

verdict.summary: congratulate_user passes a size derived from the attacker-controlled username length (18 + userName_size + 1) to snprintf instead of the actual buffer capacity (buffer_size, which is never used). With a 30-byte stack buffer in main, any username of 12 or more characters makes snprintf write past the end of buffer, an out-of-bounds stack write with attacker-controlled content.

No guard, clamp, or comparison against buffer_size exists anywhere in the code.

Exploitation requires the attacker to control the process's own argv (e.g., a setuid wrapper or a service that forwards usernames to this code); regardless, the out-of-bounds write itself is fully instantiated within this code.

verdict.summary: hash_passwords sets every salt to 32 zero bytes via std::memset instead of generating a random salt (the RAND_bytes call is commented out), so all PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 password hashes use a known constant salt: identical passwords produce identical hashes and a single precomputed rainbow table cracks every account, defeating the documented purpose of per-user salts for database storage.

Every user's password is therefore hashed with the identical, publicly predictable salt (consumed at line 35 by PKCS5_PBKDF2_HMAC and emitted by main), enabling rainbow-table attacks and cross-user password equality detection. Trigger instantiated: any invocation, e.g. './prog alice pw1 bob pw1', yields identical (hash, salt) tuples for both users.

assumptions: PKCS5_PBKDF2_HMAC behaves per OpenSSL documentation (per-discipline-3 standard-callee semantics).
limitations: count is not validated against passwords.size() inside hash_passwords; a caller passing count > passwords.size() would cause an out-of-bounds read via passwords[i]. The only caller in this code sizes both vectors from the same count (std::vector<std::string> passwords(count);), and the doc comment documents count as 'The number of passwords to hash', so the mismatch is a contract violation not instantiated by any statement of this code (CWE-125 would apply if such a caller existed).
passwords[i].length() is size_t while PKCS5_PBKDF2_HMAC takes int passlen; truncation requires a >2GB password string, not producible by any statement in this code.
usernames parameter is unused; no security effect.

verdict.summary: pcmk_process_exit is an internal daemon exit handler. verdict.summary: In SKIP_TYPE_ROW and SKIP_TYPE_COL, parse_mb_skip checks only 1 bit of availability per row/column (`if (get_bits_left(&s->gb) < 1)`) but the else arms then read s->mb_width (resp. s->mb_height) bits via get_bits1 with no per-iteration bits-left check, so a crafted WMV2 frame whose row/column flag bit is 0 drives get_bits1 past the end of the packet buffer — an attacker-controlled out-of-bounds read of decoder heap memory.

With bits_left=1 and a flag bit of 0, this line executes get_bits1 with 0 bits remaining and keeps reading past buffer_end for mb_x=1..mb_width-1 — out-of-bounds heap read fully instantiated by attacker-controlled frame payload and dimensions.

The switch has no default arm; if skip_type had a value outside the four named constants the function would return 0 with mb_type unwritten — a decode-accuracy concern with no demonstrated memory-safety impact.

The overread bits only influence MB_TYPE_SKIP flags, so direct information disclosure would require a side channel through decode behavior; the concrete instantiated impact is the out-of-bounds read itself and resulting decoder instability.

av_rescale is FFmpeg's public documented API with semantics a*b/c (division by the third argument); its body is not shown, so the SIGFPE is inferred from documented API semantics.
limitations: av_frac_add (lines 46, 50) may receive AV_NOPTS_VALUE-derived huge values via st->pts.val = pkt->dts (line 39) and the st->pts.val truthiness test (line 45); any fault there lands inside the unshown callee, so the impact chain is not instantiated here.
No memory-corruption primitive exists in this function; the confirmed defect is a division-by-zero crash (denial of service), not corruption.

verdict.summary: Resolver-derived attacker-influenced strings (LB policy name, service config JSON) reach only NULL/sentinel-checked lookups, parses, strcmp, and log arguments; the historical dangling-pointer hazard on lb_policy_name is neutralized by gpr_strdup before grpc_channel_args_destroy, and error refcounts balance on all paths.

assumptions: The caller holds chand->mu (implied by the _locked suffix); chand fields are internal-trusted callback context.

grpc_lb_policy_create returns NULL for an unregistered policy name and copies/does not retain lb_policy_args.args past the call; grpc_service_config_create returns NULL on invalid JSON; grpc_error_create_referencing tolerates GRPC_ERROR_NONE members in its refs array; grpc_lb_policy_check_connectivity sets its out-param on all paths — all unshown project-internal callee contracts relied upon, none of which guard an attacker-content sink in this code.

channel_arg->type fields and the grpc_lb_addresses array/num_addresses pairing are constructed by same-project resolver code, so DNS-supplied content cannot change arg types or the count/array invariant.
limitations: GPR_ASSERT(channel_arg->type == GRPC_ARG_STRING / GRPC_ARG_POINTER) would abort on a mistyped channel arg from an internal resolver; not attacker-instantiable (type is a producer-set struct field, not attacker data), so treated as an internal contract violation, not a vulnerability.

GRPC_ERROR_CREATE_REFERENCING is invoked with refs possibly containing GRPC_ERROR_NONE (e.g. grpc_error *refs[] = {error, state_error}; on the shutdown path, and &error in the fail_all path); a crash would require the unshown callee to mishandle NONE, which cannot be confirmed or refuted from the given code — speculative.

If an lb policy implementation retained lb_policy_args.args without copying, grpc_channel_args_destroy later in the function would leave a dangling pointer; retention behavior is in unshown callee code and is assumed to be copy-based — speculative.

verdict.summary: on_resolver_result_changed_locked consumes resolver-produced channel args (network/name-resolution-derived data) and, when GRPC_ARG_LB_ADDRESSES is present, dereferences channel_arg->value.pointer.p as grpc_lb_addresses without any NULL check: GPR_ASSERT(channel_arg->type == GRPC_ARG_POINTER) narrows only the union discriminator and if (channel_arg != NULL) guards only the arg pointer. If the resolver result carries a NULL LB-addresses pointer (in-domain for the unshown producer's void* field), the loop condition addresses->num_addresses dereferences NULL and crashes the client process — a denial of service triggered by data crossing a trust boundary.

evidence.reason: channel_arg->value.pointer.p is a resolver-result field (producer not shown; full pointer domain applies) that is assigned to addresses and immediately dereferenced in the loop condition addresses->num_addresses with no NULL check on any path. The only guards — if (channel_arg != NULL) and GPR_ASSERT(channel_arg->type == GRPC_ARG_POINTER) — constrain the arg pointer and the union type, not the payload pointer. The code checks the analogous string payloads (lb_policy_name != NULL, service_config != NULL) but has no equivalent for the pointer payload. Trigger: a resolver result with GRPC_ARG_LB_ADDRESSES of type GRPC_ARG_POINTER and value.pointer.p == NULL passes both guards, then NULL->num_addresses is dereferenced, crashing the process consuming the attacker-influenced resolver data (DoS).

assumptions: chand->resolver_result and its channel args are produced by resolver code not shown here; their content derives from network name-resolution data, so embedded fields (value.string, value.pointer.p) are treated as attacker-data under the width-domain rule.
grpc_channel_args_find is assumed to return NULL on a miss (guard at line 26 handles it) and otherwise to return a pointer to an arg of the asserted type.

grpc_error_create_referencing, grpc_lb_policy_create, grpc_lb_policy_check_connectivity, gpr_strdup, and grpc_service_config_create are internal callees not shown; their NULL/failure handling is not verifiable from the given code.
limitations: Candidate dismissed as speculative: grpc_error *refs[] = {error, state_error} passed to GRPC_ERROR_CREATE_REFERENCING when error == GRPC_ERROR_NONE (possible when the resolver is already NULL/disconnected at the else branch) may pass a NULL into the refs array; whether that is harmful depends on grpc_error_create_referencing internals (not shown), so no impact link can be instantiated.

Candidate dismissed as speculative: strcmp(lb_policy_name, "grpclb") and the %s gpr_log assume resolver-supplied strings are NUL-terminated; the producer's termination contract is not shown and the code has no local check, but instantiating a non-terminated string requires the unshown producer's behavior.
The error parameter is referenced into new errors but never GRPC_ERROR_UNREF'd in this function; whether that leaks depends on the closure error-ownership convention, which is not shown.
GPR_ASSERT(channel_arg->type == GRPC_ARG_STRING/GRPC_ARG_POINTER) aborts the process on a mistyped resolver arg; this is a deliberate documented contract assert rather than a guard defect.

The NULL LB-addresses pointer requires the (unshown) resolver to emit a GRPC_ARG_POINTER arg with a NULL payload; the trigger is instantiated only via the width-domain rule over the unshown producer's pointer field, which is why confidence is moderate rather than high.

verdict.summary: In oidc_handle_logout, the attacker-supplied logout URL reaches the redirect/query-assembly sinks only after passing the quoted validation arm (oidc_validate_post_logout_url ... == FALSE -> HTTP_BAD_REQUEST) and being escaped (oidc_util_escape_string) before embedding into the end-session URL; both statements are in execution order before every use. The front/back-channel dispatch arms pass the raw URL onward without local validation, but both the admission predicate and the downstream handling live inside project-internal callees not shown, so no trigger or impact link can be instantiated from the given code alone; per the symmetric callee rule these arms are recorded as limitations, not findings.

assumptions: oidc_validate_post_logout_url is a project-internal callee not shown; per discipline 3 its strictness could neither be credited as a guard for the pass/fail content nor assumed to pass attacker URLs, so the open-redirect trigger on the post-logout arm could not be instantiated in either direction.

oidc_util_escape_string is assumed (standard, name-documented semantics) to URL-encode its argument; its failure/NULL behavior was not quotable from the given code, but APR psprintf handles NULL %s per standard-library semantics.

oidc_is_front_channel_logout / oidc_is_back_channel_logout / oidc_handle_logout_request / oidc_handle_logout_backchannel / oidc_debug are internal callees not shown; their matching predicates, redirect behavior, and log sanitization are not quotable from this code.
c->default_slo_url, c->error_template, and provider->end_session_endpoint are treated as operator/IdP-trusted configuration rather than attacker data.
limitations: Front-channel dispatch: `return oidc_handle_logout_request(r, c, session, url);` inside `if (oidc_is_front_channel_logout(url))` passes the raw, unvalidated attacker URL to the logout handler. If oidc_is_front_channel_logout's pattern can be matched by an attacker-crafted URL and oidc_handle_logout_request redirects to its argument without state verification, this is an open redirect (CWE-601). Neither the matching predicate nor the redirect/verification behavior is shown, so the trigger is speculative in this code.

Log handling: `oidc_debug(r, "enter (url=%s)", url)` logs the raw attacker-controlled URL; if the debug callee performs no newline sanitization, log forging (CWE-117) is possible. The callee and log sink are not shown.
NULL url reaching oidc_debug's %s is at worst a formatting/robustness issue; APR-style formatters print a placeholder for NULL strings.
apr_psprintf/apr_pstrdup allocation-failure paths (NULL logout_request) are ternary-guarded before strchr and degrade to a misformatted string, not memory unsafety.

verdict.summary: The only executed memory operation, the table[i] store, is provably in-bounds: the loop bound i < 256 + 2*YUVRGB_TABLE_HEADROOM exactly matches the declared array dimension. The unvalidated inc/elemsize values feed only pointer formation (y_table -= elemsize*(inc>>9); table[i] = y_table + elemsize*(cb>>16)), which is not dereferenced anywhere in this code; any resulting out-of-range table pointer would be consumed by caller code not shown, so no impact chain is instantiated here.

assumptions: av_clip is the standard FFmpeg clamp returning a value in [0, 255]; its semantics are relied on per callee-semantics discipline.
table and y_tab are supplied by an internal static caller whose allocation/NULL behavior is not shown; no quoted precondition exists, so no candidate relies on their validity.
YUVRGB_TABLE_HEADROOM is a compile-time constant; i - YUVRGB_TABLE_HEADROOM cannot overflow int for any plausible macro value.
limitations: inc and elemsize are completely unguarded (no range check, clamp, mask, or caller-side allocation sized from elemsize*(inc>>9) appears in this snippet). With an extreme inc, av_clip(...)*inc overflows int64_t (UB) and the stored table[] pointers can point far outside the y_tab allocation — this is the shape of the historical ffmpeg swscale table-overrun bug. However, the dereference of those pointers occurs in the caller's table consumer, which is not part of the given code, so the out-of-bounds read impact cannot be instantiated from this snippet alone.

Forming y_table via y_table -= elemsize*(inc>>9) can move the pointer before the start of the underlying object, which is undefined behavior in C for extreme parameter values, but no use of that pointer executes in this code beyond re-adding offsets.

verdict.summary: The index fx returned by rpmfiNext(fi) is validated only with '>= 0' before being used to index the heap array fdata, which was allocated with exactly fc = rpmfilesFC(files) entries ('struct filedata_s *fdata = xcalloc(fc, sizeof(*fdata));'). No statement on any path compares fx against fc, clamps it, or otherwise bounds it, so any fx >= fc produced while iterating package-derived file sets makes '&fdata[fx]' point past the allocation, and the subsequent stores (e.g. 'fp->action = FA_SKIP;', 'fp->skip = ...', 'fp->stage = FILE_PRE') and reads ('!fp->skip') become out-of-bounds heap accesses with attacker-crafted package content in a root-privileged installer process.

evidence.reason: fx comes from the not-shown iterator rpmfiNext and is a full-domain int; the loop guard '(fx = rpmfiNext(fi)) >= 0' checks only the lower bound. The very next statement uses fx to form '&fdata[fx]' and the body writes through it ('fp->action = FA_SKIP;' line 26, 'fp->skip', 'fp->setmeta', 'fp->stage = FILE_PRE' line 44). With a package whose file iteration yields fx >= fc, e.g. fc = 1 and fx = 1, fp points one past the heap allocation and those stores are out-of-bounds heap writes. The identical unguarded pattern recurs at the sinks on lines 66, the setmeta loop, and the commit/erase loops; the raw index is also passed unvalidated to rpmfsGetAction(fs, fx) and setFileState(fs, fx).

The only in-code bound on the array is fc = rpmfilesFC(files) (line 10), used exclusively here for allocation (and for the cleanup free loop); it is never compared against fx at any index site. This is the allocation whose size the missing guard 'fx < fc' would have enforced.

assumptions: rpmfiNext/rpmfilesIter/rpmfiNewArchiveReader semantics are not shown; per the width-domain rule fx is treated as full-domain int, and no narrowing contract is quotable from this code.
rpm's xcalloc aborts the process on failed/overflowing allocation, so a hostile huge fc terminates rather than corrupting.
fdata is zero-initialized by xcalloc, so fp->stage comparisons against FILE_NONE assume FILE_NONE == 0.
