fsmFsPath is assumed to return an allocated string, as the cleanup loop free(fdata[i].fpath) implies.
limitations: If a caller passed a NULL failedFile, '*failedFile = xstrdup(fp->fpath)' would dereference NULL; treated as an interface-contract/robustness issue since the harmful value requires caller behavior not shown.
Possible double-free if fsmCommit(&fp->fpath, ...) frees fpath before the cleanup loop frees it again; fsmCommit is not shown, so the trigger cannot be instantiated here.
Fclose(payload)/fdOp(payload, ...) with a NULL payload from rpmtePayload (e.g. non-TR_ADDED te) depends on unshown callee NULL handling; not instantiated.
The 'worst case is a crash' dismissal does not apply to the primary finding, which is a memory-corruption primitive.

verdict.summary: The only memory-safety sink, qemu_chr_fe_write(ibe->chr, ibe->outbuf + ibe->outpos, ibe->outlen - ibe->outpos), is protected on every in-code path: the outlen == 0 check skips the sink for empty state, the only goto-send re-entry establishes (outlen=2, outpos=0) immediately beforehand, and outpos += ret cannot exceed outlen because the chardev API returns at most the requested length. No attacker-instantiable trigger for the unsigned-length wrap exists from the statements given.

assumptions: qemu_chr_fe_write follows its documented QEMU chardev semantics: returns a byte count no greater than the requested len, 0 if the backend cannot accept data, or a negative errno — never a value exceeding len
ibe->outbuf is a fixed-size struct-resident array of at least 2 bytes (compile-time property, so the constant writes outbuf[0]/outbuf[1] are in bounds)
ibe->extern_timer is created at device realize and is non-NULL when this timer-driven continuation runs
limitations: The candidate unsigned wrap of ibe->outlen - ibe->outpos (outpos > outlen causing a huge length at the write) could only be instantiated if a sibling producer in the same file (the guest-command handler that fills outbuf) set the fields inconsistently; that producer is not shown, and per the stated rules an unshown internal producer can never supply a trigger, so this remains speculative rather than a vulnerability of the given code

If a future/unshown writer of outlen/outpos violated the 0 <= outpos <= outlen invariant, the subtraction at the qemu_chr_fe_write call would wrap; a defensive outpos > outlen check would harden the sink but its absence is not exploitable from this code alone

verdict.summary: On PLATFORM_WEB the attacker-derived clipboard text is embedded into JavaScript source passed to emscripten_run_script, but the guard `if (strchr(text, '\'') != NULL) ... else emscripten_run_script(...)` rejects every text containing the single-quote byte, and U+0027 is the only character that can terminate a single-quoted JavaScript string literal (a trailing backslash merely escapes the closing quote, yielding a SyntaxError with no code execution). Simulated breakout payloads ('\u0027);evil()//', trailing '\', newline, quote) all fail to escape string context, so no code-injection trigger is instantiable. Residual issues are robustness-only: a NULL text crashes the web path in strchr (the desktop path documents NULL handling in GLFW), and clipboard content risk is inherent to the API's purpose.

assumptions: TextFormat is a raylib-internal callee not shown here; per discipline 3 its behavior (vsnprintf-style formatting into a static buffer with truncation) is an assumption that neither triggers nor protects any candidate.
emscripten_run_script evaluates the passed string as JavaScript (documented emscripten runtime semantics: eval of the string).

glfwSetClipboardString copies string data to the OS clipboard and treats NULL as clearing the clipboard (documented GLFW semantics); CORE.Window.handle is initialized elsewhere and is a data-inert argument.
limitations: CWE-476 (robustness, not a security vulnerability): if a caller passes text == NULL on a PLATFORM_WEB build, `strchr(text, '\'')` at the check line dereferences NULL and crashes the calling process; the PLATFORM_DESKTOP path handles NULL per GLFW documentation, so the API is inconsistent. Impact is a crash of the caller's own process at equal privilege with no corruption, disclosure, or bypass.
If a caller passes a non-NUL-terminated buffer, strchr and %s read past the buffer (OOB read) — an undocumented caller contract; treated as robustness.
Text containing an apostrophe cannot be set on web (function logs a warning and does nothing) — functional limitation, not security.
A trailing backslash or newline in text makes the generated JavaScript a SyntaxError, so the clipboard is silently not set — functional/DoS of a single call, no attacker code executes.
Residual clipboard-content risk (e.g., pastejacking if a user pastes attacker-controlled clipboard data into a shell) is inherent to the API's purpose and is not a defect in this code.

verdict.summary: signature_name is derived from the validated file's certificate subject (attacker-controlled content) and its byte at index len is passed directly to isspace() without an unsigned char cast; bytes 0x80-0xFF arrive as negative values, outside isspace's documented domain, causing an out-of-bounds ctype-table read on MSVC release builds (and a debug CRT abort) at a call that gates the 'expected signer' decision.

evidence.reason: Root cause: the index bound is guarded by the short-circuit `len >= strlen(signature_name)`, but the byte VALUE is not: signature_name[len] has type char (signed on Win32), and the attacker controls the certificate subject string returned by GetSignatureName, so a subject such as 'Microsoft Windows\x80...' makes strncmp(...)==0 at line 19 and evaluates isspace(-128). No cast, mask, or range check on any path (mention sweep: lines 12, 19, 20, 25, 26) narrows the byte into isspace's required domain [0, UCHAR_MAX]. On the MSVC release CRT this indexes the ctype array out of bounds; the result decides whether the signer is treated as expected (advisory suppressed).

Origin of the tainted value: the signature (certificate subject) name extracted from the file at 'path', whose content crosses a trust boundary; only the NULL sentinel is checked (line 12), the byte content is unvalidated attacker-data whose full domain is all byte values.

assumptions: GetSignatureName(path) returns the signer/subject name embedded in the Authenticode signature of the file being validated; the file content is attacker-influenced (e.g., a downloaded binary), so the returned string's bytes are attacker-data per the width-domain rule.
cert_name[] is a static internal list of expected signer names; selected_langid and hDlg are app-internal.
char is signed on the Win32/MSVC target this code is written for (WinVerifyTrust/MessageBoxExU usage).
limitations: Memory leak: signature_name is never freed on any return path (safe_free is only applied to trust_file.pcwszFilePath at line 52); bounded per call, not attacker-scalable amplification.

TOCTOU between GetSignatureName(path) and WinVerifyTrust on the same path requires a local same-privilege racing process; the window is not exhibited as two ordered operations on shared state in this code — speculative.

The unexpected-signature YESNO prompt (lines 24-29) is a deliberate user-consent advisory; the actual trust verdict is still WinVerifyTrust's return value, so the ctype defect's impact is limited to the out-of-bounds read, a possible advisory suppression, and a debug-CRT assertion abort.
The concrete out-of-bounds read depends on the MSVC release CRT's unchecked ctype table lookup; only the undefined-behavior precondition violation is guaranteed by the standard.

verdict.summary: virgl_cmd_get_capset passes the guest-controlled gc.capset_version (uint32, full-domain attacker data from the virtqueue command) unvalidated into virgl_renderer_fill_caps, while the destination buffer resp->capset_data was allocated with max_size derived from gc.capset_id alone. The code fetches the maximum supported version into max_ver but never compares gc.capset_version against it, so a guest requesting a version above the maximum directs a larger caps layout to be written into the smaller allocation — a heap out-of-bounds write (memory corruption) in the host QEMU process triggered by a malicious guest.

evidence.reason: Root cause: the guest-controlled capset_version is passed raw into the caps memory-fill operation with no validation anywhere in this code; the only local check (`if (!max_size)`) guards a different variable. max_ver, the bound fetched on lines 8-9, is never used. Trigger: guest issues VIRTIO_GPU_CMD_GET_CAPSET with a valid capset_id (max_size = caps size at the maximum supported version) and capset_version > max_ver (e.g. 0xFFFFFFFF, within its uint32 domain); the buffer allocated at line 14 is sized max_size, and the fill directed by the out-of-domain version writes past resp->capset_data + max_size — heap out-of-bounds write in the host process from guest data (CWE-787).

Origin of the defect's missing link: this statement retrieves the maximum supported version (max_ver) and its size (max_size), but max_ver is dead for the remainder of the function — no comparison of gc.capset_version to max_ver exists on any path, leaving the fill_caps sink on lines 16-18 unguarded.

Attacker-data origin: gc.capset_id and gc.capset_version are filled from the guest's virtqueue command data (gc.capset_version is uint32_t with full-domain surface per the width-domain rule); this is the trust-boundary intake point whose unvalidated value reaches the fill_caps sink.

assumptions: VIRTIO_GPU_FILL_CMD(gc) populates gc from the guest's virtio-gpu control command data (standard QEMU macro, not shown); the macro itself is treated as the trust-boundary intake, and gc.capset_version is classified attacker-data with full uint32 domain.

virgl_renderer_get_cap_set sets max_ver/max_size out-params according to the capset_id (the bound the fill must respect), and virgl_renderer_fill_caps writes caps data selected by (capset_id, version) into the caller buffer; both are project-internal callees not shown and therefore cannot serve as guards — the missing local check is the defect at the call site.
struct virtio_gpu_resp_capset ends in a flexible/variable capset_data array so sizeof(*resp) + max_size correctly sizes the allocation for max_size payload bytes.
limitations: The concrete overflow extent of virgl_renderer_fill_caps for an out-of-domain version lives inside the unshown callee; per the analysis rules this cannot demote the call-site defect, but it prevents simulation of exact bytes written.

sizeof(*resp) + max_size could wrap size_t on a 32-bit host if the unshown get_cap_set callee ever returned max_size near UINT32_MAX; no statement bounds max_size above, but the code declares no 32-bit target and the callee's size table is not shown — speculative.

If virgl_renderer_get_cap_set failed to write its out-params for an unknown capset_id, max_size would be an uninitialized stack value; the local `if (!max_size)` check covers the callee-sets-zero case, and the callee's behavior for unknown ids is an unquoted assumption — speculative.
Large max_size allocations (guest-triggerable only via the callee's fixed per-capset size table) are at most a resource-consumption concern, not an instantiated amplification.

verdict.summary: In the CMAP branch, the return value of avio_read(s->pb, pal + 4, 768) is discarded while pal_size is unconditionally set to 772 beforehand, so a truncated palette leaves up to 768 bytes of the stack buffer 'pal' uninitialized; the subsequent memcpy(pkt->data, pal, pal_size) in the FRAM/NULL branches copies this uninitialized stack memory into a demuxed packet, disclosing process stack memory through the decoder output.

evidence.reason: Root cause: the return value of avio_read is consumed by nothing (no assignment, no comparison), yet pal_size was already fixed to 768+4 on line 38. A file whose CMAP chunk is truncated causes avio_read to return fewer than 768 bytes, leaving pal[4..771] partially uninitialized (stack garbage).

Sink: copies the full 772-byte pal buffer — including the bytes left uninitialized by the unchecked read at line 40 — into the output packet delivered to the decoder (same sink also at line 31 for the NULL tag), causing disclosure of uninitialized stack memory in the demuxed frame.

assumptions: DXA_EXTRA_SIZE is assumed to be at least 9 so that AV_RB32(buf + 5) at line 47 stays in bounds (constant defined outside this code); its companion read at line 43 fills DXA_EXTRA_SIZE-4 bytes, so the access pattern is self-consistent.
The demuxed packet's palette bytes propagate to decoder output as raw frame data; the exact rendering path is outside this code.
limitations: C2 (speculative): size = FFMIN(c->bytes_left, c->bpc) at line 11 truncates a negative c->bytes_left into uint32_t 'size'; the only local guard is the truthiness test 'c->bytes_left' at line 8, which does not exclude negatives, and 'ret != size' at line 14 is checked only after av_get_packet. Whether bytes_left can be negative depends on the unshown header parser, and the consequence depends on unshown av_get_packet/av_new_packet internals, so this was not promoted.

On line 43 the failure sentinel of avio_read is correctly checked ('ret != DXA_EXTRA_SIZE - 4' returns before any use), and all packet copy offsets are compile-time constants matching the allocations at lines 28 and 52; no bounds defect exists in the FRAM/NULL paths.

The severity of the C1 finding assumes the attacker can arrange a short palette read followed by a usable FRAM/NULL chunk; the behavior of url_feof after a short avio_read is a property of code not shown here and per the analysis rules could not be used to dismiss the candidate.

verdict.summary: The archive extractor validates only entry pathnames via is_path_safe (rejecting absolute paths and '..'), but never inspects symlink/hardlink targets and configures libarchive's disk writer with only ARCHIVE_EXTRACT_TIME|ARCHIVE_EXTRACT_PERM, omitting ARCHIVE_EXTRACT_SECURE_SYMLINKS/SECURE_NODOTDOT/SECURE_NOABSOLUTEPATHS. An attacker-supplied tar containing a symlink entry (e.g., 'lnk -> /tmp/pwn') followed by a file entry 'lnk/f' passes all validation and causes archive_write_header/archive_write_data_block to create and write the file through the symlink, writing outside dest_path — an arbitrary file write leading to potential code execution.

evidence.reason: Extraction flags omit all link-safety options (ARCHIVE_EXTRACT_SECURE_SYMLINKS, ARCHIVE_EXTRACT_SECURE_NODOTDOT, ARCHIVE_EXTRACT_SECURE_NOABSOLUTEPATHS); these flags, propagated to the writer by archive_write_disk_set_options(ext, flags) at line 104, are the only mechanism that would make libarchive refuse to extract through symlinks or external hardlink targets. Their absence is the missing guard.

The only validation applied to attacker-controlled entry metadata checks the pathname string alone (leading '/' and '..' components). No statement in this code checks archive_entry_filetype, archive_entry_symlink, or archive_entry_hardlink, so a symlink entry whose target escapes dest_path (e.g., 'lnk' -> '/tmp/pwn') is accepted.

Sink: writes the attacker-controlled entry to disk without secure-link flags. Simulated trigger: entry 1 'lnk' (symlink to /tmp/pwn) creates /tmp/d/lnk; entry 2 'lnk/f' is opened through that symlink here and its data is written via archive_write_data_block (line 158) to /tmp/pwn/f, outside dest_path — arbitrary file write.

assumptions: libarchive semantics relied upon per standard documentation: without ARCHIVE_EXTRACT_SECURE_* flags, the disk writer performs plain path resolution (follows symlinks) when creating entries and does not validate hardlink linknames.
archive_entry_pathname is assumed non-NULL for tar entries produced by libarchive's reader; a NULL pathname would crash is_path_safe, but tar entries always carry a pathname.
limitations: is_path_safe fails open if strdup returns NULL: strtok(NULL, "/") then returns NULL, the loop is skipped, and the function returns true. Trigger requires an allocation failure the attacker cannot induce — robustness issue, not counted.

Two-pass TOCTOU: the archive is fully validated in a first pass (lines 115-123), freed, then re-opened from the same tar_path for extraction (lines 126-131). An attacker able to atomically replace tar_path between the two opens extracts completely unvalidated content; requires winning a local file-swap race, so recorded as a secondary TOCTOU issue rather than a primary finding.
snprintf(full_path, PATH_MAX, ...) silently truncates paths longer than 511 chars, but the retained prefix always begins with dest_path + '/', so truncation alone does not enable traversal.
ARCHIVE_EXTRACT_PERM restores full mode bits (including setuid) from the archive; this amplifies the write primitive but is part of the same defect.

verdict.summary: The faad2 frontend main() copies attacker-controlled command-line strings into fixed-size stack buffers with unbounded primitives: strcpy of argv[optind] and optarg into char[255] arrays (lines 69, 76, 196), sscanf with an unbounded "%s" into a 10-byte stack buffer (lines 83, 94, 108, 122), and an unconditional strcat of a file extension onto a possibly-full buffer (line 216). No length check, width specifier, or bounded-copy form exists anywhere in the code, so any command-line argument longer than the destination buffer causes a stack-based out-of-bounds write (memory corruption / potential code execution).

evidence.reason: Unbounded strcpy of the attacker-controlled non-option argument (full string domain of argv) into the 255-byte stack array 'char aacFileName[255];' declared at line 19. Trigger: an argument of 255+ bytes overflows the stack buffer; no strlen/snprintf/bounds check exists on any path (the argc check at line 181 bounds the count of arguments, not their length). Out-of-bounds stack write.

sscanf with an unbounded "%s" writes the first whitespace-delimited token of the attacker-controlled option argument into the 10-byte stack buffer 'char dr[10];' declared on the preceding line. Trigger: '-s' (and identically '-f'/'-b'/'-l' at lines 94, 108, 122) with a token longer than 9 characters overflows the 10-byte stack buffer before any check runs; the '< 1' test only detects an empty match, not length. Out-of-bounds stack write.

Unbounded strcpy of the attacker-controlled -o option argument into the 255-byte stack array 'char audioFileName[255];'. Trigger: '-o' with a value of 255+ bytes overflows the stack buffer; mirrored at line 76 for adtsFileName via -a. No length validation anywhere in the code.

Unconditional strcat of a file extension onto audioFileName after line 209 copies the up-to-254-character aacFileName into it. Trigger: a 248-254 character input filename with no '.' (strrchr at line 211 returns NULL, no truncation) fills the buffer, and the appended extension writes past the 255-byte boundary — an overflow reachable even for argument lengths that survive the strcpy at line 196.

assumptions: getopt_long behaves per POSIX: optarg points to a NUL-terminated substring of argv of arbitrary length, and argv[i] strings have no length limit imposed by this code.
file_ext is a global string-table indexed 1..2; the index is safely bounded by the quoted range check 'if ((format < 1) || (format > 2)) showHelp = 1;' combined with the early return at line 181-185.
limitations: fread(header, 1, 8, hMP4File) return value is unchecked, so 'unsigned char header[8]' can be partially uninitialized if the file is shorter than 8 bytes (CWE-908); the uninitialized bytes are used only for the 'ftyp' sniff and ungetc pushes, a minor robustness issue, not a promoted finding.
The eight consecutive ungetc(header[i], hMP4File) calls exceed the single-character pushback the C standard guarantees; potential UB on some libcs, robustness only.
'float dec_length = ... (clock() - begin)/CLOCKS_PER_SEC' can be 0, making 'length/dec_length' an inf/NaN float — non-faulting, no security effect.

audioFileName/adtsFileName may be uninitialized when passed to decodeMP4file/decodeAACfile if neither -o/-a nor the line-207 branch ran; the callees are not shown, so any use there cannot be judged in this code.

verdict.summary: In ProcXResQueryResourceBytes, the request-size validation computes its 'extra bytes' bound as stuff->numSpecs * sizeof(ctx.specs[0]) directly from the attacker-controlled CARD32 numSpecs field. On builds where size_t is 32 bits, numSpecs = 0x20000000 makes the product wrap to 0, so REQUEST_FIXED_SIZE passes for a request containing no spec data. The unvalidated count and the raw spec-list pointer ((char*)stuff + sz_xXResQueryResourceBytesReq) are then handed to the ctx-construction helper, which iterates/allocates from 2^29 specs that do not exist in the request buffer, causing a heap out-of-bounds read (with disclosure and server-crash potential) — the CVE-2018-14600 pattern. No range check, clamp, 64-bit intermediate, or division pre-check on numSpecs exists anywhere in the code.

evidence.reason: The sole upper-bound enforcement on the attacker-controlled CARD32 numSpecs is this size expression, and the bound itself wraps: with 32-bit size_t, numSpecs = 0x20000000 yields a product of 0 (0x20000000 * 8 = 0x100000000 truncated to 32 bits), so the fixed-size check validates only the bare header. The unvalidated count and the spec pointer just past the header (lines 12-13) then reach the ctx-construction call, iterating far beyond the heap-allocated request buffer — heap out-of-bounds read and attacker-scalable work. Root cause: integer overflow (CWE-190) in the validation expression; the missing guard is any pre-check such as numSpecs > INT32_MAX / sizeof(spec) or a 64-bit intermediate product.

assumptions: REQUEST_AT_LEAST_SIZE/REQUEST_FIXED_SIZE are the standard X-server validation macros; their bodies are not shown, so their exact comparison arithmetic (and whether a later version pre-checks (n) > INT32_MAX) is assumed from convention, not quoted.

The head of the call at lines 12-13 is truncated in the given code; it is assumed to pass stuff->numSpecs and the spec-list pointer into an initialization/allocation helper, matching the upstream AllocateConstructResourceBytesCtx call.

ConstructResourceBytes, the ctx helper, WriteFragmentsToClient, and DestroyConstructResourceBytesCtx are unshown project-internal callees; per discipline 3 their behavior cannot act as either a guard or a trigger.
Input-side byte-swapping of stuff->numSpecs for swapped clients (SProcXResQueryResourceBytes) is not part of this code; this function only swaps the reply.
limitations: The overflow trigger at the quoted sink requires a build where size_t is 32 bits (a standard deployment of the X server, but not the only one); on 64-bit builds the product cannot wrap and REQUEST_FIXED_SIZE soundly binds numSpecs to the actual request length. This is the same platform precondition as the historical CVE-2018-14600.

The concrete out-of-bounds read occurs inside the unshown ctx-construction helper; this code's defect is the wrapped validation expression and the call site passing the raw out-of-domain count/pointer, per discipline 3.

bytes_to_int32(ctx.resultBytes) truncates a callee-produced byte count into the 32-bit reply length field; since resultBytes is produced by an unshown callee and no misuse of the truncated value is shown, this is not counted as a vulnerability here.
stuff->client is an arbitrary attacker-supplied XID passed to ConstructResourceBytes as a lookup key; no harmful use of it is visible in this code.

verdict.summary: Static table-filling helper whose only memory write, `table[i] = ...`, is provably bounded by the loop guard `i < 256 + 2*YUVRGB_TABLE_HEADROOM`, which exactly matches the declared array extent, and whose clipped factor is bounded by `av_clip(..., 0, 255)`. The unguarded pointer arithmetic (`y_table -= elemsize * (inc >> 9)` and `y_table + elemsize * (cb >> 16)`) computes values that could point outside the y_tab buffer if the unshown caller passes an inc/elemsize inconsistent with that buffer, but the resulting pointers are only stored (in bounds) and never dereferenced in this code; the memory-access impact lies entirely in the unshown caller (allocation with headroom) and consumer (table dereference during scaling). No attacker-facing entry point exists here, and no local guard could even be written since the buffer size is not a parameter.

assumptions: `av_clip(x, min, max)` behaves as a standard clamp macro, returning a value in [min, max] — relied on as the guard for the first multiplicand of cb.
`YUVRGB_TABLE_HEADROOM` is a positive compile-time constant (its declaration is not shown); the loop bound and array extent agree for any positive value.

The unshown caller allocates y_tab with headroom consistent with the inc/elemsize it passes, and the unshown consumer dereferences table[] entries within that allocation — this contract cannot be quoted from the given code and therefore was not used to dismiss any memory access occurring IN this code (none occurs).
limitations: C1 (stored wild pointer, lines 6 and 9): if the unshown caller passes inc/elemsize values inconsistent with the y_tab allocation (full int domain per the width-domain rule), the pointers stored into table[] point outside the buffer. The out-of-bounds dereference happens in the unshown swscale consumer code, so the memory-corruption impact chain is not instantiated in this snippet; recorded as a caller-contract dependency, not a vulnerability of this code.

C2 (signed overflow, lines 6 and 8): `elemsize * (inc >> 9)` and `av_clip(...) * inc` are int×int multiplications assigned to a pointer offset / int64; for extreme |inc| or |elemsize| from an unshown producer they can overflow int. The overflowed values flow only into stored pointers (never dereferenced here), so impact again breaks at the unshown consumer; also, in the real FFmpeg caller inc is a small per-pixel-format constant, an unquotable narrowing that cannot be used as a guard but explains why the path is not attacker-instantiable in practice.
Robustness note: this function cannot validate its own pointer math because the y_tab buffer's size is not a parameter; a defensive fix would require an API change in the caller, not a local guard.

verdict.summary: controller::bookmark builds a shell command by string concatenation and executes it via /bin/sh -c. Only url receives any escaping (utils::replace_all(url,"'", "%27") plus literal single quotes in the format string); title, description, and feed_title are inserted bare — quote_empty(stfl::quote(...)) is a terminal-form quoting helper, not a shell escaper, and no statement of this code strips shell metacharacters. A malicious feed supplying a title such as '; cmd;' achieves arbitrary command execution when the operator bookmarks the item with bookmark-cmd configured.

evidence.reason: Sink: cmdline — built from attacker-controlled feed fields with no shell escaping — is executed via /bin/sh -c (my_argv[0..2], run_program), so any shell metacharacters in title/description/feed_title are executed as commands.
evidence.trigger: Feed item with title = '; touch /tmp/pwned;' (attacker-data, full std::string domain) and operator's bookmark-cmd set, non-interactive mode

evidence.reason: Origin: title/description/feed_title are placed into the shell command with no shell escaping; the format string "%s '%s' %s %s %s" wraps literal quotes only around the url slot, and the only escaping call in the code (replace_all on url) does not apply to these three arguments.
evidence.trigger: Same as sink: raw feed-supplied strings flow into the sh -c command line

assumptions: stfl::quote and quote_empty are project-internal callees not shown; by name stfl::quote is an STFL terminal-form quoting helper, and per analysis rules no shell-escaping behavior may be credited to it.
url, title, description, feed_title originate from remote feed/HTML content (producers not shown in this code) and are treated as attacker-data per the width-domain rule.
utils::run_program with {"/bin/sh","-c",cmdline} and utils::run_interactively execute their argument through a shell (standard execv semantics).
limitations: Minor: the DEBUG log line at line 17 writes the raw cmdline; newline-bearing feed fields could forge log entries (CWE-117) — secondary to the confirmed command injection.
Injection requires the operator to have configured bookmark-cmd and to invoke bookmarking on the malicious item; this is the feature's normal usage, not a speculative precondition.

verdict.summary: png_zalloc divides PNG_UINT_32_MAX by the caller-supplied 'size' parameter without first checking size != 0. As zlib's allocation callback taking uInt parameters whose producer is not validated anywhere in this code, size == 0 is within the declared-width input surface; the division at line 14 raises a divide-by-zero fault (SIGFPE), crashing the process that performs the allocation. The single missing guard is a zero-check on 'size' before the division; no mention of 'size' anywhere in the function performs such a check.

evidence.reason: Division by zero: the attacker-surface parameter 'size' (uInt, full-domain input of a zlib allocation callback, producer not shown/quoted in this code) is used as the divisor in PNG_UINT_32_MAX/size with no prior check that size != 0. A mention sweep of every statement referencing 'size' (line 1 declaration, line 14 divisor, line 19 multiplier) shows no zero-check, clamp, or mask on any path. Trigger: png_zalloc(ctx, items=1, size=0) → line 8 passes (png_ptr non-NULL) → line 14 evaluates 4294967295/0 → arithmetic fault, aborting the operator's process (denial of service). The check simultaneously serves as the overflow guard for line 19, so it cannot be removed without replacement; the minimal fix is a size == 0 rejection before the division.

assumptions: PNG_UINT_32_MAX is 0xFFFFFFFF (standard libpng definition); png_memset has memset semantics; png_warning's return value is void and intentionally ignored.

Outside the PNG_1_0_X build, the NULL-check on png_malloc's result (line 26) is compiled out; whether png_malloc can actually return NULL (vs. png_error/longjmp) depends on the not-shown implementation and the PNG_FLAG_MALLOC_NULL_MEM_OK flag semantics.
limitations: Unchecked png_malloc return passed to the caller outside PNG_1_0_X builds: impact depends on how the unshown consumer (zlib) handles a NULL zalloc result; no security effect is instantiable from this code alone.
p->flags is restored after png_malloc, but if png_malloc error-paths via longjmp the modified flag would persist; no attacker-reachable error path is shown in this code, so this is not instantiated.

Practical exploitation of size == 0 requires the not-shown zlib caller to invoke the zalloc callback with size == 0; per the width-domain rule for callback parameters this is treated as instantiable, which is why confidence is 0.7 rather than higher.
The overflow guard itself (items > PNG_UINT_32_MAX/size) is correctly formulated (floor-division admits exactly the non-overflowing values); the defect is solely the missing zero-divisor check.

verdict.summary: In SProcXkbSelectEvents, for size==1 event types (XkbBellNotify/XkbActionMessage/XkbCompatMapNotify) the bounds check `if (dataLeft < (size * 2))` guarantees only 2 remaining request bytes, but the `else` arm then resets `size = 2` and lines 66-67 consume 4 bytes, wrapping the unsigned `dataLeft` from 2 to 0xFFFFFFFE. Every subsequent loop iteration then passes the same check with a huge dataLeft, and swaps()/swapl() read and write 4-8 bytes past the end of the client's request buffer in the X server process — an out-of-bounds write (with out-of-bounds read) triggered by any connected X client via a crafted affectWhich bitmap and minimal request length.

evidence.reason: The only bounds guard for the swap sink compares dataLeft against size*2 evaluated BEFORE size is reset; for size==1 events it guarantees only 2 bytes remain, yet 4 bytes are consumed. Instantiated trigger: with a minimal-length request (dataLeft = 16 - 14 = 2, the struct being 14 bytes) and affectWhich bits for XkbCompatMapNotify and XkbAccessXNotify, dataLeft == 2 passes this check (2 < 2 is false) and the under-consumption is under-admitted.

Root cause: the else arm resets size from 1 to 2 after the guard, so the size==1 path advances from.c8 by 4 (already past the buffer when dataLeft was 2) and subtracts 4 from the unsigned dataLeft == 2, wrapping it to 0xFFFFFFFE. This wrapped value then satisfies the line-53 check for all later iterations, removing every bound on the swap pointers.

Sink: on the next set bit (e.g. XkbAccessXNotify, size=2), the check at line 53 sees dataLeft = 0xFFFFFFFE and passes, so swaps() read and write request bytes 18-21 while the request buffer is only 16 bytes — an out-of-bounds read+write of 4 bytes past the client's request buffer in the privileged server process (swapl at lines 60-61 gives an 8-byte variant).

assumptions: XKB protocol constants per the standard X11 XKB extension: event type ordering XkbCompatMapNotify=7, XkbBellNotify=8, XkbActionMessage=9 precede XkbAccessXNotify=10 / XkbExtensionDeviceNotify=11, so a size-1 event can precede a size-2/4 event in the ndx loop and its underflow feeds a subsequent swaps/swapl.

SIZEOF(xkbSelectEventsReq) = 14 (2 CARD8 + 6 CARD16, alignment 2), so dataLeft = req_len*4 - 14 is always ≡ 2 (mod 4); REQUEST_AT_LEAST_SIZE therefore admits req_len = 4, giving dataLeft = 2, the exact boundary value the flawed check under-admits.
swaps/swapl byte-swap in place, i.e. they both read and write the referenced memory (standard X server byte-swap macros).
XkbMapNotifyMask == (1 << XkbMapNotify), so line 26's `ndx == XkbMapNotify` skip cannot leave a bit permanently set in maskLeft and the loop terminates (every set bit is cleared at line 28).
limitations: dataLeft == 3 is unreachable because dataLeft stays ≡ 2 (mod 4); only the dataLeft == 2 boundary value triggers the underflow.

The corrupted bytes are byte-swapped copies of adjacent heap/struct memory, so the write value is not fully attacker-chosen; the offset (up to ~28 bytes past the buffer, extendable via more affectWhich bits) and which 2- or 4-byte words get touched are attacker-controlled.
The post-loop check at line 69 (`if (dataLeft > 2) return BadLength;`) rejects the request, but only after the out-of-bounds swaps have already executed, so it does not mitigate the corruption.

verdict.summary: gen_mtsr extracts the segment-register number (SR) and the GPR index (rS) from the guest-controlled instruction word and passes both to the segment-register store helper / cpu_gpr array indexing with no bounds check, mask, or clamp anywhere in the function; the only check present guards privilege (ctx->pr), not the index domain. A guest supervisor can supply an opcode whose SR field exceeds the segment-register count or whose rS exceeds the GPR array bound, yielding an out-of-bounds write of guest-controlled data inside the host emulator process (CWE-787) and an out-of-bounds translation-time array read (CWE-125).

evidence.reason: The SR number derived from the guest instruction word is passed unvalidated as the segment-register index to the store helper. Root cause: absence of a bounds check (SR must be 0-15) at this call site. Instantiated trigger: a guest supervisor executes an opcode word whose SR extraction yields 16 (one-past the 16-entry segment-register array); the emitted helper call then writes the guest-controlled GPR value out of bounds inside the host CPUPPCState — guest-to-host memory corruption.

cpu_gpr is indexed with rS(ctx->opcode) extracted from the guest-controlled opcode with no mask, clamp, or range check on any path in this code (the only check, 'if (unlikely(ctx->pr))', constrains privilege, not the index). Trigger: rS = 32 indexes one-past the GPR array at translation time — out-of-bounds read of a host global array whose result becomes a generated-code operand.

assumptions: The definitions of the SR() and rS() field-extraction macros, the size of cpu_gpr, and the internals of gen_helper_store_sr are not shown; per the analysis rules their bounding effects cannot be quoted and therefore cannot serve as guards — their absence from the given code is treated as absence of validation at this use site.

ctx->opcode is assumed to be filled from guest instruction memory by the decoder (not shown); the guest VM is the trust-boundary party, so any value the instruction word can represent is instantiable.
tcg_const_tl is assumed not to return a failure sentinel consumed by this code; t0 is used at line 12 and freed at line 13 with matching lifetime.
limitations: In the real QEMU source these opcode-field macros are masked to the architectural field widths (rS to 5 bits, SR to 4 bits) and the guest instruction encoding itself cannot express an out-of-range field; under that (unquoted) code both candidates collapse to non-issues. The vulnerable verdict is relative to the given snippet alone, judged as the last line of defense.

If the not-shown helper gen_helper_store_sr internally validates the segment-register number, the OOB write (CWE-787) is prevented downstream; per the rules the unvalidated raw-index pass at the call site is still recorded as the defect, but this link is an assumption rather than a quoted statement, which is why confidence is moderate.
No missing-CPU-model/CPU-feature validation (e.g., mtsr legality on 64-bit implementations) can be assessed here; the opcode dispatch table that gates instruction availability is not shown.

verdict.summary: jpc_pi_nextrpcl computes the precinct index pi->prcno = prcvind * numhprcs + prchind from attacker-controlled JPEG-2000 codestream geometry (sampling factors, precinct exponents, reference coordinates) with no range validation against pi->pirlvl->numprcs, then uses it to index the prclyrnos array (pi->pirlvl->prclyrnos[pi->prcno]) for both a read and an increment write. The only bound-related statement, assert(pi->prcno < pi->pirlvl->numprcs), is compiled out under NDEBUG and omits the lower bound, so an out-of-bounds read followed by an out-of-bounds write (++(*prclyrno)) occurs at an attacker-scalable offset in the process decoding the crafted image.

evidence.snippet:
pi->prcno = prcvind * pi->pirlvl->numhprcs + prchind;

assert(pi->prcno < pi->pirlvl->numprcs);
evidence.reason: Root cause: prcno is computed from attacker-controlled codestream values (prcvind, prchind derived from hsamp/vsamp, prcwidthexpn/prcheightexpn, xstart/ystart, and the loop-walked x/y) with no runtime range check. The only bound mention, assert(pi->prcno < pi->pirlvl->numprcs), is removed under NDEBUG, lacks a lower-bound arm, and is not an enforcement guard. Nothing ties numhprcs/numprcs (produced by unshown allocation code) to the precinct span actually walked by the x/y loops, so prcno can exceed numprcs.

Sink: prcno (unvalidated, per the missing check at line 81) indexes the numprcs-sized prclyrnos array. Simulated trigger: numrlvls=1, r=0, prcwidthexpn=0, hsamp=vsamp=1, xstart=ystart=0 passes the alignment gate for every x, giving prchind = x and prcno = x; once x >= numprcs, *prclyrno is an out-of-bounds read and ++(*prclyrno) is an out-of-bounds write at an offset scaling with the attacker-chosen image width — memory corruption in the decoding process.

assumptions: All pi fields consumed here (pchg progressions, numcomps, hsamp/vsamp, numrlvls, prcwidthexpn/prcheightexpn, numprcs, numhprcs, prclyrnos, xstart/ystart/xend/yend, numlyrs, maxrlvls) are populated by the unshown JPEG-2000 decoder from the attacker-supplied codestream; per the width-domain rule each is treated as attacker-data over its declared width, and no unshown decode-layer validation is credited.

prclyrnos is allocated elsewhere sized by numprcs (unshown); per discipline 3 this unshown sizing neither guards the index nor proves consistency between numhprcs/numprcs and the locally computed prchind/prcvind.
Release builds define NDEBUG, so the assert at line 83 is absent; per standard assert semantics this is treated as a non-guard.
limitations: Secondary candidate (not verdict-driving): if a component's hsamp or vsamp is 0 (or the shift/product at lines 36-39 wraps to 0), pi->xstep/pi->ystep remain 0 and lines 50/52 (pi->y % pi->ystep, pi->x % pi->xstep) divide by zero — a SIGFPE crash of the decoding process (CWE-369). Trigger requires the unshown parser to admit a zero sampling factor; recorded as a denial-of-service/robustness issue, not memory corruption.

Secondary candidate (not verdict-driving): a negative pchg->compnostart (full int domain, producer unshown) passes the loop condition at line 55 (pi->compno < pi->numcomps) and is dereferenced at line 57 (pi->picomp->numrlvls), giving an out-of-bounds read just below the picomps array (CWE-125); trigger requires the unshown parser to admit a negative POC component start.

Negative prcno is not reachable from this code alone: x >= xstart and y >= ystart with monotone CEILDIV/FLOORDIVPOW2 keep prchind/prcvind >= 0; the confirmed defect is the upper-bound violation (prcno >= numprcs).

verdict.summary: jpc_pi_nextrpcl computes the precinct index pi->prcno from attacker-controlled codestream fields (x/y coordinates, sampling factors, resolution exponents, numhprcs) at line 72 and uses it to index the heap array pirlvl->prclyrnos at line 77 without any enforced bounds check: the only mention, assert(pi->prcno < pi->pirlvl->numprcs), is compiled out under NDEBUG and checks only the upper bound. A malformed JPEG-2000 codestream (e.g., prcwidthexpn=prcheightexpn=0 with numhprcs=numprcs=1 and yend>1) drives prcno=1, and ++(*prclyrno) at line 79 writes an int past the end of the heap buffer (heap corruption, CVE-2016-8691 family). Independently, pi->xstep/pi->ystep can be 0 when an attacker sets hsamp/vsamp=0 (lines 29-34 have no nonzero check), causing a division by zero at pi->x % pi->xstep (line 45) — a reachable denial of service.

evidence.reason: This assert is the ONLY statement in the code constraining pi->prcno before it indexes prclyrnos. It is not an effective guard: it is removed when NDEBUG is defined, and it checks only the upper bound (no prcno >= 0). pi->prcno = prcvind * pi->pirlvl->numhprcs + prchind (line 72) is built entirely from attacker-controlled codestream fields with no relation enforced between numhprcs, prcvind and numprcs, so out-of-range values are instantiable.

Out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). Simulated trigger: with prcwidthexpn=prcheightexpn=0, hsamp=vsamp=1, numrlvls=1, numhprcs=numprcs=1, second y iteration gives prcvind=1, pi->prcno = 1*1+0 = 1 at line 72; the assert at line 74 provides no runtime bound in release builds, so prclyrnos[1] is dereferenced one element past the heap buffer and ++(*prclyrno) writes an attacker-positioned int out of bounds. No bounds check, clamp, mask, or error arm on prcno exists on any path (mention sweep: lines 66-72 compute, 74 asserts, 77 indexes, 79 writes).

Division by zero (CWE-369). pi->xstep/pi->ystep are computed at lines 29-34 as picomp->hsamp * (1 << (...)) and JAS_MIN-propagated with no nonzero validation anywhere (lines 23, 29-33, 42-45 are the only mentions). An attacker-supplied component with hsamp=0 (or vsamp=0) makes pi->xstep==0, and pi->x % pi->xstep evaluates a division by zero, terminating the decoder process parsing the attacker's file — a reachable denial of service.

assumptions: All pi fields (pchg progression fields, xstart/ystart/xend/yend, hsamp/vsamp, numrlvls, prcwidthexpn/prcheightexpn, numprcs/numhprcs, prclyrnos array, numcomps, maxrlvls, numlyrs) originate from JPEG-2000 header parsing not shown in this snippet; per the width-domain rule they are treated as attacker-data spanning their full declared widths, since no quoted statement of this code narrows them.
assert is assumed to follow standard C semantics: it is a no-op when NDEBUG is defined, which is the normal release configuration for library builds.

JPC_CEILDIV/JPC_FLOORDIVPOW2/JAS_MIN/JAS_CAST are taken as standard ceil-division, floor-shift, min, and cast macros; their arithmetic cannot re-bound prcno below numprcs without a check on numhprcs vs numprcs, which is absent.
limitations: Line 46-48 computes pi->picomp = &pi->picomps[pi->compno] with pi->compno = pchg->compnostart BEFORE the loop condition, and the condition (pi->compno < JAS_CAST(int, pchg->compnoend) && pi->compno < pi->numcomps) has no lower bound; a negative compnostart (full int domain of the attacker-derived POC field) yields an out-of-bounds read at pi->picomp->numrlvls on line 50 (CWE-125). Confirmed by simulation but not driving the verdict per the two-CWE cap.

Shift counts at lines 29-32 (prcwidthexpn/prcheightexpn + numrlvls - rlvlno - 1) are attacker-derived ints with no local cap; large values cause undefined-shift behavior that can additionally zero xstep/ystep, feeding the CWE-369 path.

The goto skip at line 21 re-enters the innermost loop without re-running the outer-loop initializations; this is a deliberate resumable-iteration idiom relying on prior pi state and was not found to bypass any guard relevant to the confirmed defects.

verdict.summary: hfile_mem_get_buffer computes the reported buffer length as `file->buffer - file->limit`, which is the reverse pointer difference (buffer start minus one-past-the-end). For any memory-backed hFILE with nonzero capacity this yields a negative ptrdiff_t that wraps to a huge size_t (e.g. capacity 4096 -> 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFF000). The exported API therefore returns the correct buffer pointer paired with a wildly wrong length; any consumer that copies, reads, or allocates based on *length performs a massively out-of-bounds operation. No clamp, check, cast, or error arm anywhere in the code bounds this value.

evidence.reason: Reversed pointer subtraction: file->limit is one past the end of the hFILE buffer and file->buffer is its start, so the difference is -(capacity); assigning this negative ptrdiff_t into the size_t output wraps modulo 2^64 to ~SIZE_MAX. Trigger: any valid mem-backend hFILE (backend check at line 2 passes), length non-NULL (line 7 passes), capacity > 0. No guard in the code bounds, clamps, or corrects the computed value, so the caller receives a corrupted length that directly sizes memory operations on the returned buffer.

assumptions: hFILE field semantics (buffer = buffer start, limit = one-past-the-end, limit >= buffer) follow the htslib hfile internal layout; the producers of these fields are not shown, and per the width-domain rule any representable pointer values are instantiable — the wrap occurs for every state with limit > buffer.
hfile_mem_get_buffer is an exported API whose documented contract is to return the memory file's buffer and its length; consumers use *length to size copies/reads of the returned buffer.
limitations: Passing a NULL `file` dereferences it at line 2 (`file->backend`), but this only crashes the caller's own process at equal privilege with no corruption, disclosure, or bypass — robustness issue, not a vulnerability.
A zero-capacity mem file yields *length == 0 (correct only by coincidence of the wrap); the defect manifests for every capacity > 0.

The concrete memory-safety consequence (out-of-bounds copy/read sized by the wrapped length) executes in the caller, which is not shown; the defect proven here is the wrapped size value itself delivered by the exported length output.

verdict.summary: png_zalloc dereferences png_ptr (via p->flags) before the NULL check executes, causing a NULL-pointer dereference crash when the zalloc callback is invoked with a NULL png_ptr; independently, the overflow check divides by size without any zero test, causing an integer division-by-zero crash when size == 0. Both parameters are callback intake-point arguments (zlib zalloc) with no quoted narrowing statement in this code, and the code itself anticipates png_ptr == NULL (line 8), proving NULL is in-domain. Impact: crash/DoS of the process consuming attacker-influenced image data.

evidence.reason: NULL pointer dereference (CWE-476): png_ptr is dereferenced via p->flags at line 5, but the only NULL guard, 'if (png_ptr == NULL) return (NULL);' at line 8, executes AFTER the first use, so it does not cover it. The code's own line-8 check proves NULL png_ptr is an anticipated in-domain callback input; with png_ptr == NULL, line 5 reads p->flags at offset from address 0 and crashes the process before the guard is reached. No statement in execution order between entry and line 5 validates png_ptr.

Division by zero (CWE-369): the overflow check divides PNG_UINT_32_MAX by size with no zero test anywhere in the code (mention sweep of size: lines 1, 10, 15 — none is a zero-check, clamp, or mask). size is a uInt callback parameter whose full width domain includes 0; when size == 0 the expression SIGFPE-crashes the process before any return path. Note: for size >= 1 the same check correctly prevents the items*size overflow, so the defect is solely the unguarded divisor.

assumptions: PNG_UINT_32_MAX is 0xFFFFFFFF and png_uint_32 is a 32-bit unsigned type, as in standard libpng.
png_zalloc is installed as zlib's zalloc callback; per the width-domain rule its parameters (png_ptr, items, size) are attacker-data by default because no statement in this code narrows them.

PNG_1_0_X conditional zero-fill block: the NULL sentinel of png_malloc is checked at line 22 before any memset, and the num_bytes > 0x8000L strict comparison is correct at both bounds — no defect there.
limitations: Practical reachability of png_ptr == NULL or size == 0 depends on the unshown caller (zlib) passing such values; zlib's documented zalloc protocol may never do so, but that contract is not quotable from this code and per the rules cannot serve as a guard. If the caller contract were enforced elsewhere, both findings would reduce to robustness issues in this function.
Impact is process crash (denial of service) only; no memory corruption, disclosure, or bypass path was instantiated from these defects.

verdict.summary: ff_h264_pred_weight_table() iterates `for (i = 0; i < ref_count[list]; i++)` using an attacker-influenced, unvalidated reference count (full int domain) and writes parsed weights into the fixed-size arrays pwt->luma_weight[i][list][k] and pwt->chroma_weight[i][list][j][k], including duplication writes at indices 16+2*i and 16+2*i+1. No statement in this code bounds ref_count[list] or i against the array dimensions, so any count exceeding the arrays' capacity causes an out-of-bounds write of partially attacker-controlled integers in the host process parsing the H.264 bitstream.

evidence.reason: Missing-check site: ref_count[list] is attacker-data (int parameter of an exported bitstream parser; its producer is not shown, so its surface is the full int domain) and is used directly as the loop bound. The mention sweep found only two mentions of ref_count (the declaration at line 2 and this bound); no bounds check, clamp, mask, or early-reject exists anywhere in the function. Trigger: ref_count[0] = e.g. 0x1000 lets i run far past the fixed first dimension of pwt->luma_weight/pwt->chroma_weight, making the stores at lines 31/42/50/64 out-of-bounds writes.

Sink: with picture_structure == PICT_FRAME the code duplicates weights to indices 16+2*i and 16+2*i+1; the index scheme is designed for i <= 15, so any ref_count above that (and any large ref_count in general) writes attacker-influenced integers out of bounds of the fixed-size H264PredWeightTable arrays. The written values come from get_se_golomb() (range-limited to int8_t by the check at lines 33-35) or the defaults luma_def/0, giving a partially controlled, repeatable OOB write primitive.

Taint origin: ref_count enters as a const int * parameter whose producer is not shown in this code; per the width-domain rule every value representable in int for each list element is instantiable, and no quoted statement of this code narrows it.

assumptions: The struct definition of H264PredWeightTable is not shown; its luma_weight/chroma_weight first dimensions are finite compile-time constants (the code indexes them with [i][list][j] as in-struct arrays). The trigger holds for any finite dimension because the attacker-controlled count's declared domain (int) exceeds it.
slice_type_nos, sps->chroma_format_idc and picture_structure are treated as attacker-influenced parse-derived values; they only select branches and do not themselves index memory.
limitations: Dismissed: luma_log2_weight_denom / chroma_log2_weight_denom are guarded by the quoted checks `> 7U` with clamp-to-0 (lines 11-14, 18-21); edge-tested at 7 (allowed, 1<<7=128 fits int), 8 (rejected), and ue(v) values that wrap to negative int (promoted to unsigned in the comparison, rejected).
Dismissed: parsed weight values are range-guarded by the quoted int8_t casts at lines 33-35 and 52-54 with a goto out_range_weight error arm that precedes all later consumption.
Dismissed: chroma_def is only used inside quoted `if (sps->chroma_format_idc)` blocks (lines 45, 73), so the uninitialized-when-idc==0 case never reaches a use.

In the upstream project the caller (slice-header decoding) clamps ref_count to the maximum reference count; that enforcement is not shown here and per the guard-anchoring rule cannot demote the missing local validation at this intake point.
The exact array dimension being overflowed is not quotable from the given code; the out-of-bounds conclusion depends only on it being finite, which the fixed struct indexing implies.

verdict.summary: Heap out-of-bounds read in chmd_read_headers: for PMGL entries whose filename begins with '::' (system files), the code unconditionally compares fixed lengths (31 bytes at name[2], and 8/11/72 bytes at name[33]) against the content/control/spaninfo/rtable names, while the only name_len checks permit name_len as small as 2. A crafted CHM chunk places a 2-byte '::' entry near the end of the chunk-size-byte heap buffer, so mspack_memcmp reads up to ~28 bytes past the allocation. The name_len bound (`name_len > (unsigned int)(end - p)`) constrains only p+name_len <= end, never the fixed memcmp read lengths.

evidence.reason: Heap OOB read (CWE-125): the memcmp is specified to read 31 bytes starting at name[2] (name[33]-based memcmps below read up to 104), but name_len is only checked to be >= 2 (line 195) and to fit within end-p (line 188). Trigger: crafted CHM with chunk_size=64, num_chunks=1, first_pmgl=last_pmgl=0 passes all quoted header guards; a PMGL chunk carries a padding entry followed by an entry with name_len=2, name='::' at offset 50, so name[2]=chunk[52] and memcmp reads chunk[52..82], up to 19 bytes past the 64-byte sys->alloc'd chunk buffer; attacker-controlled in-chunk bytes matching content_name force the read to proceed past the allocation.

evidence.snippet:
if (name_len > (unsigned int) (end - p)) goto chunk_end;
      name = p; p += name_len;
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted pointer 'name' and the only name_len bound: it guarantees p+name_len <= end (i.e., the entry name fits within the chunk) but does not bound the fixed 31-byte read at &name[2] nor the name[33]-relative reads, so a name_len=2 '::' entry near the end of the chunk reaches the memcmp block unguarded.

assumptions: READ_ENCINT macro and constants (pmgl_Entries, content_name, control_name, spaninfo_name, rtable_name, *_SIZEOF offsets) are not shown; pmgl_Entries and the system-name lengths taken from upstream libmspack where they are 0x14 and 39/42/39/105-byte constants — the defect does not depend on their exact values, only on the memcmp lengths (31/8/11/72) exceeding the enforced minimum name_len of 2.
sys->read/alloc/seek/copy/message semantics per the mspack_system interface: read returns bytes read, alloc returns pointer or NULL (NULL is checked at line 157 and 209).
limitations: Line 95: `chm->sec0.offset = chm->dir_offset + (chm->chunk_size * chm->num_chunks);` can overflow int*int for version<3 files, and the wrapped value can pass the `sec0.offset > length` check; sec0.offset has no memory sink in this function, impact would land in later extraction code not shown.

Line 165: `(int)chm->chunk_size` truncates when chunk_size > INT_MAX (possible since chunk_size is only bounded by attacker-set file length); a negative read size's behavior depends on the unshown sys->read implementation, but the symmetric `(int)` cast in the comparison makes short reads fail into MSPACK_ERR_READ.

first_pmgl/last_pmgl are never validated against chm->num_chunks and `x * chm->chunk_size` is computed in wrapping unsigned arithmetic before the seek; worst case is extra failed reads (MSPACK_ERR_READ) or a wrong seek position, no corruption in this code.

verdict.summary: The -s, -f, -b, and -l option handlers copy the attacker-supplied command-line token into a 10-byte stack buffer using unbounded sscanf("%s"), so any argument token longer than 9 characters writes out of bounds on the stack (memory corruption), with no width bound anywhere in the code.

evidence.reason: Unbounded sscanf %s writes optarg's entire token plus NUL into the 10-byte stack buffer dr; a token of length >= 10 (e.g. `faad -s 1111111111X`) overflows the stack frame — out-of-bounds write of attacker-controlled bytes. No width modifier, length check, or clamp exists on any path (mention sweep: only `if (optarg)` NULL test and a post-hoc return-count test, neither bounds the copy).

Same unbounded sscanf %s into 10-byte stack dr for the -f option; attacker argument `-f <10+ chars>` triggers the stack out-of-bounds write before the format range validation at lines 111-112 ever runs.
Same unbounded sscanf %s into 10-byte stack dr for the -b option; attacker argument `-b <10+ chars>` triggers the stack out-of-bounds write.
Same unbounded sscanf %s into 10-byte stack dr for the -l option; attacker argument `-l <10+ chars>` triggers the stack out-of-bounds write.

assumptions: getopt_long supplies optarg per its documented semantics; optarg content and length are fully attacker-controlled command-line data.

file_ext[] is a global table with entries for format indices 1..2, matching the validated range at lines 111-112; the -o/-a/aacFileName strcpy paths are sized from the identical strlen expressions they copy and were verified safe.
limitations: Line 262 `fread(header, 1, 8, hMP4File);` — return value unchecked; for an input shorter than 8 bytes, header[4..7] are uninitialized stack garbage consumed by the mp4-detection at line 267 and the ungetc calls at lines 277-284 (CWE-457/CWE-908). Trigger instantiated (e.g. empty input file), but the observable consequence (which decoder path is taken) lands entirely inside unshown callees decodeMP4file/decodeAACfile, so no corruption, disclosure, bypass, or amplification is provable from this code; not counted as primary.
Repeated -o/-a options leak the previously allocated audioFileName/adtsFileName — resource leak only, no security impact.
`progName = argv[0]` (line 37) can be NULL under exotic exec conditions and floats point to float division by zero yielding inf rather than a fault — robustness only.
The duplicate {"stdio", 0, 0, 'w'} / {"stdio", 0, 0, 'g'} long-option entries make --stdio unmatchable to 'g'; cosmetic.

verdict.summary: The logout URL taken from the request parameter is validated for same-origin only when apr_uri_parse produces a non-NULL hostname: the check at lines 39-41 is conditional on (uri.hostname != NULL), so any URL whose authority the server-side parser does not populate (e.g. 'https:/evil.com', a single-slash or scheme-relative form) skips hostname validation entirely, passes the CR/LF check, and is used as the post-logout redirect target (directly at the final oidc_handle_logout_request call, or embedded as post_logout_redirect_uri). Browsers normalize such forms to a full authority on another host, yielding an open redirect (CWE-601).

evidence.reason: Root cause: the same-origin validation of the attacker-controlled logout URL is short-circuited when uri.hostname == NULL (urls that apr_uri_parse accepts but for which it does not populate an authority, e.g. 'https:/evil.com'). Trigger: attacker sends ?logout=https:/evil.com; apr_uri_parse returns APR_SUCCESS with hostname NULL (line 28 passes), the whole hostname check is skipped, the CR/LF check passes, and the raw url is passed as the redirect target via 'return oidc_handle_logout_request(r, c, session, url);' or embedded as post_logout_redirect_uri; browsers normalize the value to https://evil.com/, producing an open redirect.

Origin of the tainted value: the logout redirect URL is read from the HTTP request parameter; its full domain (any NUL-terminated string) is attacker-controlled at this trust-boundary intake point, and it flows unvalidated for origin to the redirect sink whenever the hostname check is skipped.

assumptions: oidc_handle_logout_request (callee not shown) is treated as redirecting the browser to its url argument, based on this code's own structure: it is called with the raw attacker url at line 12 and with the constructed logout target (default_slo_url or end_session_endpoint with post_logout_redirect_uri) at the final return; this assumption was used only to characterize the sink, never to guard it.

oidc_get_current_url_host is assumed to return the request host (possibly with port); if it includes a port while uri.hostname does not, the strstr mutual-containment check over-rejects (functional, not a security bypass, since mutual substring containment implies string equality).
Escaping of the error text echoed via oidc_util_html_send_error (lines 29-34, 42-49) is not shown; XSS there is not confirmed.
limitations: Minor: the raw logout parameter is logged at line 9 (oidc_debug) before the CR/LF validation at line 53, allowing possible log forging (CWE-117) when debug logging is enabled; not part of the verdict.

The strstr pair (lines 40-41) is case-sensitive and does not account for ports, which can cause legitimate same-host logout URLs to be rejected (functional over-rejection), but mutual substring containment prevents any bypass when hostname is non-NULL.
Impact of the open redirect is limited to post-logout phishing/misdirection; it does not directly leak session credentials in this function.

verdict.summary: GlyphCache::Loader consumes TtfUtil::GlyphCount's return (attacker-controlled maxp numGlyphs) with no validation. When the attacker's font reports zero glyphs, `_num_glyphs_graphics-1` underflows to -1 (widened to a huge size_t) and is passed unchecked as the raw glyph index into the table-indexing call TtfUtil::LocaLookup, driving an out-of-bounds access of the attacker-supplied loca table inside the host font-rendering process. The only local check is the post-hoc `== size_t(-2)` test of the callee's return, and the sole range check (`_num_glyphs_graphics > tmpnumgattrs`) executes after the call.

evidence.reason: Root cause: integer underflow at the sink. `_num_glyphs_graphics-1` is evaluated when `_num_glyphs_graphics` is 0 (attacker sets maxp numGlyphs to 0, so TtfUtil::GlyphCount returns 0), producing -1 (or an all-ones value after widening), which is passed as the raw glyph index into LocaLookup, an indexing operation over the attacker-controlled loca table. The mention sweep shows no zero/range/clamp/mask check on `_num_glyphs_graphics` before this line (lines 9 and 19 only produce the value; the range check at line 49 executes after the call), so the out-of-domain index reaches the lookup unguarded, causing an out-of-bounds read in the process parsing the malicious font.

Taint origin: the glyph count is taken from the attacker-controlled maxp table via TtfUtil::GlyphCount with no sentinel, zero, or range check on the returned value before it is decremented and used as an index at line 21.

assumptions: Member declarations (_num_glyphs_graphics, _num_attrs) are outside the given snippet; under any integer width, 0 is representable, so the GlyphCount=0 trigger stands regardless of the exact type.

TtfUtil::LocaLookup's parameter types are not shown; per the width-domain rule the passed underflowed value is treated as attacker-domain data and the callee's internal behavior may neither guard nor excuse the call site.

be::read<T> is assumed to advance the pointer by sizeof(T) (standard big-endian reader semantics); Face::Table::operator bool/size() and Face::operator bool are taken as documented table-validity/size accessors.
The `== size_t(-2)` comparison implies LocaLookup's documented out-of-range sentinel is size_t(-2); whether it can return other failure sentinels (e.g., -1) is unshown.
limitations: tmpnumgattrs arithmetic (lines 42-45) can wrap unsigned when 2*_num_attrs exceeds the remaining Gloc bytes, but on two's-complement targets the implementation-defined conversion yields a negative int that the quoted `tmpnumgattrs < 0` check rejects; escaping would require a multi-gigabyte Gloc table plus adverse conversion behavior — speculative, not a finding.

Line 69 `_has_boxes = true;` forcibly enables box parsing regardless of Glat flags; any resulting downstream misparse of Glat box data occurs in code not shown, so its impact is not instantiated here.

Only the size_t(-2) sentinel of LocaLookup is tested; other failure sentinels would pass unnoticed, but the return value is not consumed as an offset within this constructor, so no local memory-safety consequence was provable.

verdict.summary: The SMK header parser sizes the frm_size array with unchecked 32-bit attacker-controlled arithmetic (smk->frames * 4) after a bounds check that only logs and does not return, so a crafted file with frames = 0x40000001 makes av_malloc(4) succeed while the fill loop performs ~10^9 sequential out-of-bounds heap writes of attacker-controlled 32-bit values, yielding deterministic heap corruption.

evidence.snippet:
if(smk->frames > 0xFFFFFF) {
        av_log(s, AV_LOG_ERROR, "Too many frames: %i\n", smk->frames);
evidence.reason: The only bound on the attacker-controlled frames field (origin: smk->frames = get_le32(pb)) is this check, whose error arm merely logs and contains no return, so frames values up to INT_MAX proceed to the allocation and fill loops.

Root cause: the allocation size is computed with 32-bit int multiplication of the attacker value; for frames = 0x40000001 the product 0x100000004 truncates to 4, so a 4-byte buffer is allocated for 1073741825 four-byte entries; the av_malloc result is also never NULL-checked anywhere in the code.

Sink: with i bounded only by smk->frames (line 33) and the 4-byte allocation from line 29, the second iteration writes attacker-controlled data at byte offset 4 past the heap buffer and continues for ~10^9 iterations — a fully instantiated out-of-bounds heap write (CWE-787).

assumptions: SmackerContext fields (frames, treesize, etc.) are 32-bit integers as implied by get_le32 assignments and int arithmetic; int is 32 bits on the target.
av_malloc behaves as a standard allocator: returns a pointer for small sizes (e.g. 4 bytes) and may return NULL for huge requests.
get_le32/get_buffer/get_byte read from the attacker-supplied file and return 0/past-EOF behavior without aborting.
limitations: Secondary crash-grade defects not driving the verdict: av_new_stream NULL dereference at smk->indexes[i] = ast[i]->index (line 60) and the if (!st) arm at line 39 lacking a return before st->index (line 40) — NULL-deref DoS only, trigger is the in-domain allocation-failure sentinel.

Line 73-77: the !extradata error path frees and logs but has no return, so get_buffer is called with extradata == NULL + 16 (e.g. treesize = 0x30000000); the write lands at a fixed near-NULL address — crash-grade wild write, secondary to the primary heap overflow.
The magic check at line 10 has no rejecting arm, so non-SMK2/SMK4 data is parsed; no direct memory-safety impact shown.
Potential division-by-zero in av_reduce when attacker pts_inc == 0 depends on unshown callee semantics; not evaluated.

verdict.summary: Attacker-controlled feed/article metadata (url, title, description, feed_title) flows verbatim — only single quotes are replaced — into a debug LOG call, allowing a malicious feed publisher to inject newlines and forge entries in the operator's log file. Shell command injection was considered and refuted: single-quote wrapping plus replace_all(x, "'", "%27") provably prevents quote break-out in the /bin/sh -c command line.

evidence.reason: Unguarded log-injection sink: cmdline contains attacker-controlled feed/article text whose only transformation is replacement of single quotes (lines 12-15); newline characters pass through untouched and are written to the log, letting a feed publisher forge log records (e.g. title = "x\n[...] ERROR: ..."). No statement on any path sanitizes control characters before this call.

Origin of the tainted data: these handler parameters carry RSS feed / article content produced outside this code; per the width-domain rule their full std::string domain (including newlines) is instantiable by a trust-boundary party (the feed publisher).

assumptions: utils::replace_all behaves as its universally understood name implies: it replaces every occurrence of "'" with "%27", leaving all other characters (notably \n, \r, NUL, $, `, ;) intact.
LOG is a logging macro whose characterizable semantics are to emit the formatted message to the configured log destination without sanitizing embedded control characters.
cfg.get_configvalue / get_configvalue_as_bool return the local operator's own configuration values (bookmark-cmd, bookmark-interactive), which the feed publisher cannot influence.
The log sink is reachable when the operator has logging enabled at debug level.
limitations: Shell command injection was analyzed and refuted: after utils::replace_all(x, "'", "%27") each value contains no single quote, and the format string "%s '%s' '%s' '%s' '%s'" wraps each value in literal single quotes; under POSIX sh semantics no character inside '...' is special except the closing quote, so $, `, ;, \ and newlines remain literal arguments and cannot break out. The single-anomaly candidate is neutralized by this quoted guard on both the run_interactively (line 22) and /bin/sh -c (line 29) paths.
A NUL byte in attacker data truncates the sh -c command string at cmdline.c_str() (line 29), at worst producing a local shell syntax error — robustness only, no injection or corruption.
The %27 substitution mangles the bookmarked URL/title text (data corruption), which is functional, not a security impact.
Log-forging impact is limited to misleading log content; severity is low.

verdict.summary: continue_send passes struct fields outpos/outlen (set by producers not shown, so full-domain per the width-domain rule) unvalidated into a memory read: qemu_chr_fe_write(ibe->chr, ibe->outbuf + ibe->outpos, ibe->outlen - ibe->outpos). No path in this code checks outpos <= outlen or outlen <= sizeof(outbuf); if outpos > outlen the unsigned subtraction underflows to a near-2^32 length and the pointer lands past outbuf, causing an out-of-bounds read whose bytes are transmitted to the connected chardev peer (information disclosure) or a host-process crash. The only entry check, if (ibe->outlen == 0), bounds only the zero-length case.

evidence.snippet:
ibe->outpos += qemu_chr_fe_write(ibe->chr, ibe->outbuf + ibe->outpos,
                                     ibe->outlen - ibe->outpos);
evidence.reason: Root cause: the memory-read call consumes attacker-surface struct fields outpos (offset) and outlen (size) with no local bounds check on any path. Trigger (width-domain instantiated): outlen=1, outpos=0x10000 skips the line-3 zero-check, so the callee receives pointer outbuf+0x10000 and length 1-0x10000 = 0xFFFF0000 (unsigned underflow), reading out of bounds and transmitting the bytes to the external chardev peer; the only guard if (ibe->outlen == 0) does not bound outpos, and the line-9 comparison if (ibe->outpos < ibe->outlen) executes only after the read has already occurred.

assumptions: outpos/outlen are unsigned integers and outbuf a fixed-size array declared in the (not shown) device header; the defect does not depend on the exact width, only on the absence of any quotable bound relating outpos, outlen, and sizeof(outbuf).
qemu_chr_fe_write semantics per discipline 3: returns bytes written (at most len) or a negative error sentinel; it reads the supplied buffer and forwards contents to the chardev peer.
limitations: Candidate C2 (unchecked negative return of qemu_chr_fe_write added to unsigned outpos, wrapping it to 0xFFFFFFFF) is NOT exploitable in this code as written: the wrapped value fails the unsigned test if (ibe->outpos < ibe->outlen) at line 9 and the else branch resets outlen=0 and outpos=0 before any further use; it is a robustness/logic issue (a command send can be silently dropped), not memory corruption.

Whether a bad outpos/outlen state is actually reachable depends on the producers in the rest of the device file (not shown); per the analysis rules this cannot demote the missing local validation at the sink, but it lowers confidence in real-world reachability.

parse_errors: no valid JSON verdict found in output

verdict.summary: hopen_mem's own logic is fully guarded: the ',' sentinel is checked before data is derived, the ';base64' prefix read is protected by the exact-width bound 'comma - url >= 7' (correct operator, edge-tested at both bounds), both malloc NULL sentinels are tested before the decode calls, and hfile_init_fixed's NULL return is checked before dereference. The only theoretical risks — the base64 decoder writing past the buffer sized by hts_base64_decoded_length, or a callee-produced 'length' exceeding 'size' — occur entirely inside not-shown internal callees to which this code passes only in-domain arguments (a checked malloc pointer and an in-bounds NUL-terminated substring), so neither the trigger nor the impact chain can be instantiated from the given code; they are recorded as limitations, not vulnerabilities.

assumptions: hopen_mem is a static scheme handler registered for the 'data:' URL scheme; its caller (the hfile dispatch layer, not shown) passes a non-NULL url and a non-NULL mode string — these are interface contracts of the enclosing library, not attacker-triggerable in this code.

hts_base64_decoded_length returns a size that upper-bounds what hts_decode_base64 writes, and hts_decode_percent never expands its input beyond strlen(data) — internal callee contracts not shown; per the rules they are NOT relied on as guards, only recorded.
hts_decode_base64 and hts_decode_percent always set *length before returning, so the uninitialized 'length' (line 3) is written before its single use at line 26; also an unshown-callee contract.
hfile_init_fixed consumes (buffer, length, size) consistently when length <= size; its internal behavior is not shown.
limitations: Speculative (callee-mediated heap overflow, CWE-787/120): the buffer passed to hts_decode_base64 at line 16 is sized by the sibling unshown function hts_base64_decoded_length, and the capacity 'size' is never passed to or checked against the decoder's output anywhere in this code — if the unshown callee pair were ever inconsistent, a heap overflow would occur inside the callee. No trigger or impact link could be instantiated from the given code, so this is a design dependency, not a confirmed vulnerability here.

Speculative (unchecked callee output, CWE-125/457): 'length', produced by the unshown decoders, is passed to hfile_init_fixed at line 26 with no local 'length <= size' check; a mismatch would corrupt/read out-of-bounds only inside the not-shown callee.
Speculative (integer wrap, CWE-190): 'size = strlen(data) + 1' at line 19 wraps only for a near-SIZE_MAX string, which cannot exist in the address space.

Robustness: an empty base64 payload ('data:;base64,') yields size from hts_base64_decoded_length(0); malloc(0) may return NULL, making a valid empty resource indistinguishable from an OOM error. No security impact.

verdict.summary: The USB completion callback ehci_async_complete_packet re-reads the guest-writable PORTSC register at completion time and, on a guest-set POWNER bit, forwards the in-flight packet to s->companion_ports[port->index] and immediately dereferences it via companion->ops->complete with no NULL or validity check anywhere in the code. A guest that flips PORTSC_POWNER while an async packet is in flight on a machine without a companion controller registered for that port drives companion == NULL, causing a NULL-pointer dereference and crash of the host QEMU process (guest-triggered denial of service); the forwarding also passes an EHCIQueue-embedded packet into a foreign controller's callback with no validation.

evidence.reason: Root cause: unchecked use of the companion pointer at the indirect call site. s->companion_ports[port->index] is loaded with no NULL/validity check and immediately dereferenced (companion->ops) and invoked. Instantiated trigger: guest writes PORTSC[i] with POWNER=1 (guest-writable register bit, tested at line 6) while a packet is in flight, and no companion controller is registered for the port (NULL is within the field's full pointer domain) → NULL dereference → host QEMU process crash, a cross-trust-boundary denial of service.

Origin of the taint: the guest-controlled PORTSC_POWNER bit of the guest-writable MMIO register field s->portsc is re-read at completion time rather than being captured at packet submission, opening the ownership-flip race window that selects the unguarded companion-forwarding branch.

assumptions: port->opaque and port->index are set once by not-shown controller/bus initialization code that no trust-boundary party can modify via registers; they are treated as internal-trusted, and the array reads s->portsc[port->index] / s->companion_ports[port->index] carry no bounds check in this code.
PORTSC is the guest-writable EHCI port status/control register and POWNER is a documented R/W bit (public EHCI register interface); the guest can set it at any point while a packet is in flight.

s->companion_ports entries are populated by not-shown companion-controller registration; entries for ports without a registered companion remain NULL (standalone EHCI configuration), which is within the field's declared pointer domain.
The packet pointer is assumed to be the same packet submitted through the port (USB-core contract, not shown); container_of at line 11 presupposes every arriving packet is EHCIQueue-embedded.
limitations: Forwarding the EHCIQueue-embedded packet to a registered companion controller's complete handler is a potential type confusion (each controller's callback derives its own queue structure from the packet), but the companion's complete handler is not shown and cannot be characterized, so the memory-corruption impact chain is not instantiated here.

container_of(packet, EHCIQueue, packet) has no identity/liveness validation; the assert at line 13 does not verify packet identity or queue liveness, is compiled out under NDEBUG, and runs after q is already dereferenced at lines 11-12 — but a forged/dangling-packet trigger requires the not-shown USB core / queue-free path.

port->index has no bounds guard in this code (potential OOB read of s->portsc / s->companion_ports), but its producer is same-component init code not writable by any trust-boundary party, so no trigger is instantiated.
