q->usb_status = packet->len stores an unvalidated device-supplied length/error code; its consumer is not shown, so no impact link is instantiated.

verdict.summary: The evidence-index validation uses `idx <= area->evidence().size()` instead of `<`, admitting the one-past-the-end index, which is then passed to area->deleteEvidence(idx) causing an out-of-bounds removal; additionally argv[0] is accessed without any argc/argv-size check, giving an out-of-bounds read on a zero-argument packet. Both are remotely triggerable by any connected client in an evidence-enabled area.

evidence.reason: Off-by-one bounds check: the `<=` operator admits idx == evidence().size(), the one-past-the-end index of the evidence list (valid indices are 0..size-1). A client sending the equal-to-size index passes the check and reaches area->deleteEvidence(idx), which performs a list removal at an out-of-range index — an out-of-bounds destructive access (element one-past-end destroyed/shifted) in the server process. The only guard on idx is this line; no clamp, mask, or secondary check exists anywhere in the function.

argv[0] is dereferenced with no validation that argv is non-empty: the argc parameter declared on line 1 is never checked, and no argv.size()/isEmpty() guard exists anywhere in the function. A client sending the packet with zero arguments produces an empty argv, and indexing element 0 of an empty QList is an out-of-bounds read (Q_ASSERT-only in debug, undefined behavior/null-pointer dereference in release) on which toInt is then invoked — a remotely triggered crash/out-of-bounds read in the server.

assumptions: area->deleteEvidence is an unshown internal callee; it is assumed (per its name and the size() bound on the same evidence list) to remove the element at the given index, which requires the index to be within [0, size-1]; per the analysis rules the defect stands at the call site regardless of any internal check not shown here.
checkEvidenceAccess is an unshown internal callee; the trigger assumes it returns true for evidence-enabled areas, which is the feature's normal operating path.

argv is a parameter of a packet-handler intake point; per the width-domain rule its surface includes the empty list, since the unshown packet dispatcher's behavior cannot be relied on to guarantee a minimum argument count.
limitations: The exact memory-corruption primitive of the out-of-range deleteEvidence depends on the unshown removal implementation (QList::removeAt-style UB); if the unshown callee happened to internally bounds-check, the impact of the first finding would degrade to a no-op rather than corruption, though the missing local validation at the call site remains the defect in this code.

verdict.summary: No attacker-instantiable security defect found. The only raw memory-copy sink (strcpy/strcat in the 'CC +' case) is provably bounded: the allocation `malloc (strlen (comment) + strlen (newcomment) + 2)` is sized from the exact strcpy source and the pre-unescape length of the strcat source, and `r_str_unescape` is an in-place shrink-only transform of a strdup of that same string, so the worst-case write exactly fits the buffer including the NUL byte. All input[] reads are prefix-guarded by the switch dispatch (each case guarantees the preceding characters exist, so the next index is at worst the terminator), all format strings are literals, all callee failure sentinels (comment, cmtfile, text, out, newcomment, fcn) are checked before first use, and remaining concerns (OOM-only unchecked strdup results, empty-input dispatch contract, undo-entry command replay, undo_new copy semantics) have uninstantiable triggers or impact links outside this code.

assumptions: r_str_unescape performs an in-place, shrink-or-equal decode of the buffer produced by strdup(newcomment) (standard radare2 semantics; the function is not shown, and per the width-domain discipline it may not be assumed to expand to create a trigger either).
r_core_undo_new copies the strings passed as `b` and `a` before this code's `free (a); free (b);` (callee not shown).

The command dispatcher calls this handler only with input equal to the command minus its leading 'C', so input[1] of the shortest form reads the NUL terminator; an empty input would read one byte past the string.
getcommapath returns a heap pointer suitable for free and non-NULL for r_cons_printf %s.
limitations: Stored command injection: `char *b = r_str_newf (CC %s@0x%08..., nc, addr)` embeds the raw (unescaped) attacker-controlled comment into a future undo command string. No statement in this code executes that entry; the replay lives in the not-shown undo executor, so the impact chain is not instantiated here.
`char *nc = strdup (newcomment); r_str_unescape (nc);` and `s = strdup (s + 1);` use the results without NULL checks — reachable only under allocation failure (OOM), not attacker-inducible.

`switch (input[1])` and the input[2]/input[3] reads are safe for every dispatchable command form evidenced by the case comments, but a bare empty-string dispatch (caller contract not shown) would read one byte past the string buffer; command buffers in the caller make even that a non-crashing overread at worst.
`int i` compared against `bb->size` in the CCf- loop could wrap if analysis ever constructed a basic block larger than INT_MAX; the producer of such a block is not in this code.
Passing a possibly-NULL `comment` to `r_core_editor (core, NULL, comment)` relies on that callee accepting NULL initial content.

verdict.summary: The packet handler indexes argv[0] without verifying that the attacker-supplied argument list is non-empty. A remote client can send a remove-evidence packet with zero arguments, making the QList::operator[] access out-of-bounds — an OOB read/invalid index that crashes (or corrupts reads in) the shared server process. The subsequent idx bounds check on deleteEvidence is correct but never reached with an empty list.

evidence.reason: argv is an attacker-controlled QStringList (network packet arguments) whose producer is not shown; its surface includes the empty list. argv[0] is accessed with no check of argc or argv.size() anywhere in the function (mention sweep: argv/argc appear only in the signature and at this use), so QList::operator[](0) on a size-0 list performs an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) and the subsequent toInt dereference crashes the process. Trigger: any connected client sends a 'RE' packet with no arguments.

assumptions: area->evidence() and AreaData::deleteEvidence are internal callees; their behavior is not shown, but the line-7 guard 'is_int && idx < area->evidence().size() && idx >= 0' locally bounds idx to valid indices, so that use is safe.

checkEvidenceAccess is an unshown internal authz check; treated as fail-closed per 'if (!checkEvidenceAccess(area)) return;' — it does not gate the argv[0] access either way, so the defect is reachable regardless.
limitations: The exact heap layout reached by the out-of-bounds read depends on the Qt build (Q_ASSERT in debug aborts; release reads past the QList storage), so the precise impact beyond a reliable DoS (OOB read → crash of the shared server) is not further characterized here.

verdict.summary: In the replacement-copy loop of _php_mb_regex_ereg_replace_exec, the byte length `fwd` returned by php_mb_mbchar_bytes_ex(p, enc) is used directly as the copy length in out_buf.append(p, fwd) without any local check that fwd is positive or that i + fwd <= replacement.size(). An attacker-supplied replacement string ending in a truncated multibyte lead byte (e.g. a lone 0xC2 under UTF-8, or 0xF0 for a 4-byte overread) makes the append copy past the end of the replacement buffer; the overread bytes are returned in the function result, giving an out-of-bounds read with disclosure potential. The only mention of fwd before the sink is the equality probe `fwd == 1` at the backref test, which does not bound it.

evidence.reason: Sink: fwd is used as the copy length from p (inside replacement.data()) with no guard bounding it to the remaining bytes. Trigger: replacement = "\xc2" (size 1) with UTF-8 encoding; php_mb_mbchar_bytes_ex returns 2 for the UTF-8 lead byte, (replacement.size() - i) >= 2 fails at i=0, and append copies 2 bytes from a 1-byte buffer, reading past the replacement buffer; the overread bytes are returned via out_buf.detach().

Origin of the tainted length: fwd is the return of an unshown internal callee consumed with no sentinel/range check (no check for <= 0, no clamp against replacement.size() - i) before its use as a copy length at line 101 and as the pointer/increment step at lines 102-103.

assumptions: php_mb_mbchar_bytes_ex is not shown; per the width-domain rule its int return is treated as unvalidated attacker-reachable surface (a value of 2-6 for a multibyte lead byte is within any plausible encoding-length semantics and within the declared int width); no assumption is made that it clamps to the remaining buffer.
MBSTRG(current_mbctype) is a runtime-settable PHP setting (mb_regex_encoding()), so the multibyte encoding `enc` used to compute character lengths is attacker-influenced.
pattern/replacement/str/option are parameters of the exported mb_ereg_replace engine function; PHP scripts routinely pass user-derived data as the replacement, so their content is attacker-data.
onig_search is a known library: a successful forward search returns match offsets within [start, end], which underpins the guarded backref copy (lines 92-96) and the pre-match append (line 80).
limitations: If php_mb_mbchar_bytes_ex could return 0 (invalid lead byte under some encoding tables), lines 101-103 would loop forever (p and i never advance) causing a hang; this depends on unshown callee behavior and is not counted as the primary defect.

Line 113 `pos++` can push pos to string_lim+1 only if onig_search returned an empty match with start == end, which its forward range semantics do not admit; additionally the quoted guard `if (string_lim - pos > 0)` (line 117) blocks any negative-length append on the nomatch path, so this boundary concern is not instantiated.
`regs = onig_region_new()` (line 62) is not NULL-checked; allocation-failure-only trigger with no attacker induction, robustness issue only.
The backref copy at lines 95-96 is correctly guarded by `regs->beg[n] >= 0 && regs->beg[n] < regs->end[n] && regs->end[n] <= str.size()` combined with `n >= 0 && n < regs->num_regs`; no defect there.
The `e` (eval) modifier is explicitly rejected at lines 54-55 via throw_not_supported, so no code-execution path exists here.

verdict.summary: ValidateSignature is a defensive Authenticode validation routine: the only memory-index sink (isspace(signature_name[len])) is provably in-bounds via the short-circuit guard '(len >= strlen(signature_name)) || ...'; all callee sentinels (GetSignatureName NULL, utf8_to_wchar NULL, loop-exhaustion i >= ARRAYSIZE, MessageBox != IDYES) are checked in execution order, and every error path returns a failure code while success is only ever WinVerifyTrust's genuine result. No trigger with a security impact could be instantiated.

assumptions: GetSignatureName (unshown) returns a NUL-terminated string or NULL; strlen/strncmp on signature_name rely on this
cert_name[] is a fixed, non-empty array of NUL-terminated literal strings defined elsewhere
lmprintf formats come from fixed message resources (MSG_283/284/285); signature_name is only ever a %s argument, never a format string
utf8_to_wchar returns an allocated WCHAR string or NULL (its NULL sentinel is checked here)
limitations: trust_data.dwProvFlags = WTD_REVOCATION_CHECK_CHAIN | 0x400 uses an undocumented magic flag bit; no documented WinVerifyTrust dwProvFlags equals 0x400 (WTD_HASH_ONLY_FLAG is 0x200), so a CWE-347 'verification disabled' impact could not be instantiated from given code or documented semantics; the VERIFY_V2 signature check with whole-chain revocation is still invoked and its real result returned. Recommend replacing 0x400 with a named flag for auditability.
signature_name is never passed to safe_free; if GetSignatureName allocates, this is a small one-shot memory leak (CWE-401) per validation, not attacker-scalable retention

isspace(signature_name[len]) receives a plain char; for non-ASCII (negative-signed) subject bytes this is UB/misclassification, but it only affects which cosmetic whitelist prompt is shown — WinVerifyTrust remains the actual security gate, so no verification bypass results

the attacker-controlled certificate subject is echoed into uprintf/log and a MessageBox (potential CWE-117 log forging); the trigger requires the unshown GetSignatureName to pass raw CR/LF through and X.509 DirectoryString encoding to permit them — unprovable from the given code, so not a primary finding

verdict.summary: cmd_meta_comment handles attacker-controlled command text, but every memory/copy/format sink is either sentinel-checked in this code (r_meta_get_string results guarded by 'if (comment)', r_str_between by 'if (cmtfile && *cmtfile)', r_core_editor by 'if (out)', sdb_decode by 'if (s)') or provably sized: the malloc(strlen(comment)+strlen(newcomment)+2) buffer that is filled with strcpy(comment)+' '+strcat(nc) is safe because nc is strdup(newcomment) mutated only in place by r_str_unescape/r_str_ansi_strip (single char* argument, discarded void return), so strlen(nc) cannot exceed strlen(newcomment); worst case is an exact fit. No trigger for any candidate is instantiable from the code shown.

assumptions: input is a NUL-terminated string of at least one character when the (not shown) command dispatcher invokes this static handler; a bare 'C' command is handled by the dispatcher's own switch, so this function never receives an empty string from shown behavior.
r_str_unescape and r_str_ansi_strip mutate their argument in place: each is called with a single char* whose return value is discarded, so strlen(nc) <= strlen(newcomment) at the strcat sink.
r_meta_get_string, r_str_between, r_core_editor, and sdb_decode return NUL-terminated strings or a NULL failure sentinel; every consumption in this code is preceded by a quoted NULL/emptiness check.
r_num_math returns a ut64 used only as a metadata address key (r_meta_set/r_meta_del), not as an array index, so its full ut64 domain is harmless here.
limitations: Speculative: switch (input[1]) would read one byte past the terminator if a caller passed an empty string (e.g., a bare 'C' command); no such call site exists in the given code and the trigger could not be instantiated.

Fragile sizing asymmetry (not a triggerable defect): in case '+'/' ', the buffer is sized with strlen(newcomment) but the concatenation appends nc (the unescaped, ANSI-stripped copy). Safety rests on the shown strdup(newcomment) allocation capping nc's capacity and on the in-place, shrink-only nature of the two transform callees; if a future implementation expanded the string this would become a heap overflow (CWE-131 pattern), but no in-domain value overflows it as written.

Environment-failure-only robustness issues (not attacker-inducible): p = strchr(s, ' ') dereferences s without checking the preceding strdup(s + 1) for NULL in case 'a'; getcommapath/core, r_str_newf, and r_core_undo_new results are consumed without NULL checks; these fail only on allocation failure.

Case ' ' stores the attacker comment nc inside an undo command string (r_str_newf ("CC %s@0x%08"PFMT64x, nc, addr)); any command-injection impact would occur during later undo re-execution in code not shown and at the operator's own privilege, so the impact chain is not instantiated here.

verdict.summary: In nfs3svc_decode_writeargs, the received-data-length validation `if (dlen < XDR_QUADLEN(len)*4) return 0;` is computed with wrapping u32 arithmetic: for attacker-supplied len in {0xFFFFFFFD, 0xFFFFFFFE, 0xFFFFFFFF} (set via `len = args->len = ntohl(*p++);`), XDR_QUADLEN(len) = ((len+3)>>2) wraps to 0, so the check compares dlen < 0 and always passes regardless of how little data the request actually carried. The subsequent clamp `if (args->count > max_blocksize) { args->count = max_blocksize; len = args->len = max_blocksize; }` executes after the bypassed check and cannot restore the invariant that received data must cover the specified length. The decoder then returns success with args->count, rq_vec[], and args->vlen describing up to max_blocksize bytes (built via the loop `while (len > rqstp->rq_vec[v].iov_len) { ... rq_vec[v].iov_base = page_address(rqstp->rq_pages[v]); ... }`), pointing at pages the request never filled. The NFSv3 write handler consequently copies up to max_blocksize bytes of stale/uninitialized kernel memory into a file the attacker can read back (memory disclosure), or dereferences stale/NULL page pointers (kernel crash) — an attacker-triggerable integer-overflow validation bypass at a network trust-boundary decoder.

evidence.reason: This is the only data-presence guard for the attacker-controlled u32 len, and its arithmetic wraps: with len = 0xFFFFFFFD (attacker-set, after passing `if (args->count != args->len) return 0;`), XDR_QUADLEN(len) = ((len+3)>>2) = 0, so the test degenerates to `dlen < 0`, which is never true for the unsigned dlen — the request is accepted even with dlen == 0. Execution then reaches the clamp (lines 40-43) which sets count/len to max_blocksize and the vector loop (lines 47-53) which builds rq_vec/args->vlen over ~max_blocksize/PAGE_SIZE pages of rq_pages that the request never populated, and `return 1;` exports these to the write handler: out-of-bounds/stale-memory read feeding kernel memory disclosure or a stale/NULL page dereference. The missing guard is an overflow-safe comparison (e.g. `if (len > dlen) return 0;`), which appears nowhere on any path.

Origin of the tainted value: len is read directly from the network-supplied XDR stream (NFSv3 WRITE argument), with full u32 domain 0..0xFFFFFFFF and no local narrowing; len = 0xFFFFFFFD instantiates the wrap trigger at the line-37 check.

assumptions: XDR_QUADLEN(l) is the standard kernel macro ((l)+3)>>2 from include/linux/sunrpc/xdr.h (not shown in the snippet); the trigger depends on this u32 wrap at l >= 0xFFFFFFFD.

decode_fh, xdr_decode_hyper, svc_max_payload, page_address, and the fields head->iov_len / rq_arg.page_len / tail->iov_len / rq_pages[] are produced by code not shown; their bounds behavior is not relied upon for the primary trigger.

The downstream nfsd3 write handler consumes args->count, rq_vec[], and args->vlen without a re-validation shown in this code; this decoder is the intake point for the WRITE call, so per the intake-point rule the missing validation here is the defect and is not deferred to that consumer.
limitations: Secondary path: `dlen = head->iov_len + rqstp->rq_arg.page_len + tail->iov_len - hdr;` (line 28) and `rqstp->rq_vec[0].iov_len = head->iov_len - hdr;` (line 45) can also underflow if a truncated call makes hdr exceed head->iov_len, bypassing the same check by wrapping dlen huge; instantiating this requires the unshown decode_fh/RPC receive layer to deliver a head shorter than the decoded NFSv3 header and the two out-of-bounds-read words count/len to compare equal, so it is not counted as a primary candidate.

The concrete disclosure (stale/uninitialized page content written to the attacker-readable file) or the stale/NULL-page crash materializes inside the write handler (not shown); the locally proven defect is the overflow-bypassed validation and the success return exporting count/vlen/rq_vec values unbacked by received data.

verdict.summary: All attacker-controlled values (message length, clipboard flags, per-format lengths) reaching this code's memory and stream sinks are bounded by quoted checks in execution order: `if (len < 4)` rejects short/negative messages before the flags read; `if (len > maxCutText)` bounds the message; `if (len < (rdr::S32)(4 + 4*num))` exactly bounds the caps-branch reads (tested at len == 4+4*num, which fits exactly); and `if (lengths[num] > (size_t)maxCutText)` bounds each provide-branch length before `buffers[num] = new rdr::U8[lengths[num]]; zis.readBytes(buffers[num], lengths[num])`, where the allocation is sized from the identical expression as the copy length. The 16-entry arrays are index-safe via the `i < 16` loop bounds and the accept-counter `num`, and the delete loop's count provably matches the allocated set after rejected bits are cleared (`flags &= ~(1 << i)`). Remaining concerns (heap overflow inside the unshown ZlibInStream callee historically known as CVE-2024-1525, exception-path buffer leaks, stream desync from an over-declared caps length, a %d/unsigned log mismatch) all have impact chains that break inside code not given or have no security effect, and are recorded in notes.limitations.

assumptions: `maxCutText`, `clipboardActionMask`, `clipboardCaps`, `clipboardProvide`, `clipboardRequest`, `clipboardPeek`, `clipboardNotify` are compile-time constants whose declarations are not shown; they are treated as fixed positive constants.

The semantics of project-internal callees not shown (`rdr::InStream::readU32/skip`, `rdr::ZlibInStream::setUnderlying/readU32/readBytes/skip/flushUnderlying`, and the `handler->handleClipboard*` callbacks) are assumptions; per the analysis rules they can neither produce a trigger nor serve as a guard. In particular, whether `ZlibInStream` throws or misbehaves when asked to decompress more data than the underlying `len - 4` bytes can supply cannot be determined from the given code.

Whether `handler->handleClipboardProvide(flags, lengths, buffers)` retains or frees the buffer pointers (which this code subsequently `delete[]`s) is not shown; the simulated delete-count consistency assumes the handler does not take ownership.
limitations: C4 (speculative, not a vulnerability in this code): if `rdr::ZlibInStream` (not shown) mishandles requests exceeding the available decompressed data, `zis.readBytes(buffers[num], lengths[num])` could crash or overflow inside that callee — the historical TigerVNC CVE-2024-1525 pattern. In this code the passed length is bounded by `if (lengths[num] > (size_t)maxCutText)` and the destination buffer is allocated from the identical expression, so the arguments are in-domain and the harmful use, if any, occurs entirely inside the unshown callee.

C5 (speculative): if `zis.readBytes` or `zis.skip` throws mid-loop (e.g., decompression overrun), `buffers[0..num-1]` allocated earlier in the loop leak, since no RAII or cleanup exists on the exception path; the throw and post-exception process behavior both rest on unshown code.

C6 (no security effect): the caps branch permits `len > 4 + 4*num`, leaving up to `len - 4 - 4*num` bytes of the declared message unconsumed, which desynchronizes the message stream; the attacker could send those bytes as legitimate messages anyway, so no capability is gained.
C7 (cosmetic): `vlog.error("... (%d bytes) - ignoring", (unsigned)lengths[num])` uses a %d format with an unsigned argument; log text only, constant format string, no injection.

verdict.summary: SProcXkbSelectEvents validates attacker-controlled request length via REQUEST_AT_LEAST_SIZE before computing dataLeft, and guards every in-place byteswap with 'if (dataLeft < (size * 2)) return BadLength;' executed in order before each swap; the loop's only boundary mismatch (size==1 events check 2 bytes but consume 4) cannot underflow because dataLeft is always a multiple of 4 (length is an integer count of 4-byte units, SIZEOF(xkbSelectEventsReq)=16, decrements are 4 or 8), so the mismatched bound never under-admits an instantiable value and every swap remains inside the request buffer.

assumptions: REQUEST_AT_LEAST_SIZE(xkbSelectEventsReq) has its documented dix semantics: it returns BadLength when stuff->length*4 < sizeof(xkbSelectEventsReq) (and for over-large lengths), guaranteeing length >= 4 words and thus dataLeft >= 0.

The X server request dispatcher delivers each dispatched request with a buffer of at least stuff->length*4 bytes (universally known core behavior of ReadRequestFromClient); without it no X request handler could be judged.
swaps()/swapl() perform in-place 2/4-byte byte-swaps (writes back into the buffer), and SIZEOF(xkbSelectEventsReq) = 16 (4-byte header + six CARD16 fields), consistent with X protocol 4-byte padding.
limitations: Boundary mismatch at size==1 events (XkbBellNotify/XkbActionMessage/XkbCompatMapNotify): the guard 'if (dataLeft < (size * 2))' demands only 2 bytes while the else branch reassigns size=2 so 4 bytes are consumed (from.c8 += 4; dataLeft -= 4). This would underflow dataLeft if dataLeft could be 2 or 3, but dataLeft is provably always a multiple of 4 (stuff->length*4 - 16, decrements of 4 or 8), so the state dataLeft==2/3 is never instantiable from any CARD16 length value; recorded as a latent (currently unreachable) off-by-bound, not a vulnerability.

Potential dataLeft unsigned underflow if stuff->length < 4 words (length*4 < 16) would yield a huge dataLeft and far out-of-bounds heap read/write via swaps/swapl; this is blocked only by the REQUEST_AT_LEAST_SIZE macro invocation, whose semantics are a documented-framework assumption recorded above. If that macro's semantics were violated, the code would be critically vulnerable (heap out-of-bounds read/write).

The size==1 event path performs no byteswap on its own detail fields and advances 4 bytes per such event, which is a functional/protocol-accounting quirk (conservative over-consumption), not a memory-safety defect.

verdict.summary: The picture-position validation `if (s->mb_x >= s->mb_width || s->mb_y >= s->mb_height)` bounds only the upper end of the attacker-controlled macroblock coordinates set by the (unshown) picture-header decoders. Negative s->mb_x or s->mb_y values — within the full int domain of the producing callee per the width-domain rule — pass this check, make `mb_pos = s->mb_y * s->mb_width + s->mb_x` negative, and inflate `left = s->mb_width * s->mb_height - mb_pos`, so the COUNT check also passes. The decode loop then drives ff_update_block_index/ff_h263_decode_mb/MPV_decode_mb at negative macroblock coordinates, writing decoded picture data out of bounds (before the picture planes), yielding memory corruption in the decoder process from a crafted media stream.

evidence.reason: Missing lower-bound validation: this is the only positional check on the attacker-influenced s->mb_x/s->mb_y (set by the unshown header decoder), and it rejects only mb_x >= mb_width / mb_y >= mb_height. With s->mb_x = -1, s->mb_y = 0 (any negative value is in the declared int domain of the unshown producer), the check passes, mb_pos becomes -1, left is inflated to mb_width*mb_height+1 so `mb_count > left` also passes, and the macroblock loop executes `ff_update_block_index(s)` and `MPV_decode_mb(s, s->block)` at a negative coordinate, writing decoded macroblock data out of bounds before the picture buffer. The one-line guard whose absence is the defect (`s->mb_x < 0 || s->mb_y < 0`, or a non-negative check on mb_pos) appears nowhere in the code; the only statement that ever rewrites s->mb_x/s->mb_y (line 30) is skipped when current_picture_ptr is NULL.

Origin of the tainted values: the picture-header decoder (not shown) parses the attacker-supplied bitstream into s->mb_x, s->mb_y, s->pict_type and returns mb_count; only mb_count is range-checked here (lines 11, 22), while the mb_x/mb_y fields it sets are consumed as picture-plane indices with only the one-sided upper-bound test at lines 15-16.

assumptions: rv10_decode_picture_header/rv20_decode_picture_header, ff_update_block_index, ff_h263_decode_mb, MPV_decode_mb, ff_er_add_slice, MPV_frame_start internals are not shown; per the width-domain rule s->mb_x/s->mb_y are treated as full-domain int inputs, and per the call-site rule the out-of-bounds write landing inside MPV_decode_mb does not break the impact chain since the raw indices are consumed at this code's call sites after validation owned by this code.
s->mb_width/s->mb_height are assumed positive, normal decoder dimensions; the trigger uses mb_x=-1, mb_y=0, mb_count=3 with a fresh frame (current_picture_ptr == NULL).
limitations: buf_size*8 in init_get_bits (line 6) can overflow int for |buf_size| >= 2^28, but triggering it requires a >=256MB packet and the post-decode `s->gb.size_in_bits < get_bits_count(&s->gb)` checks force an error return before any corruption; overreads stay within the API-mandated input padding. Not instantiated as a vulnerability.

The size-extension hack (lines 77-79) sets s->gb.size_in_bits = 8*buf_size2 beyond the buf_size-declared extent, but the actual allocation behind buf is nowhere established in this code (buf_size2 plausibly describes additional bytes of the same buffer per an unquotable caller contract), so an out-of-bounds read cannot be fully instantiated here.

s->mb_x-1 can be -1 at ff_er_add_slice (line 100) when mb_count == 0 with mb_x == 0 or after a wrap on the final iteration; whether this is harmful depends entirely on unshown ff_er_add_slice internals (which may clip end indices), so the impact chain is not instantiated.
A NULL buf with nonzero/zero buf_size would at worst NULL-dereference the decoding process itself at equal privilege — robustness, not a security impact.

verdict.summary: qcrypto_cipher_decrypt passes the caller-controlled length 'len' directly into nettle decryption operations (cbc_decrypt at lines 14-16, alg_decrypt at lines 10-11) without verifying it is a multiple of the cipher's block size or otherwise constraining it. No statement anywhere in the function mentions 'len' except the two sinks. A non-block-aligned length from a guest VM's encrypted-disk I/O path reaches nettle's CBC routine, which is only defined for block-aligned lengths, crashing the QEMU host process (guest-triggerable denial of service); on the ECB path the trailing bytes of the output buffer are silently left uninitialized while the function returns success.

evidence.reason: Attacker-instantiable length 'len' (size_t, full domain per width-domain rule; producer not quoted in this code) is passed unvalidated to nettle cbc_decrypt, whose CBC operation is defined only for lengths that are a multiple of block_size (ctx->niv). The mention sweep for 'len' covers only its declaration (line 4) and the two uses (lines 11, 16); no check, clamp, mask, or error arm anywhere in the function constrains it. A guest issuing a non-block-aligned length on an encrypted volume aborts the host QEMU process — a denial-of-service impact at minimum.

evidence.snippet:
ctx->alg_decrypt(ctx->ctx_decrypt ? ctx->ctx_decrypt : ctx->ctx_encrypt,
                         len, out, in);
evidence.reason: Same unvalidated 'len' on the ECB path: the nettle block-decrypt callee processes only complete blocks, so trailing bytes of the caller's output buffer are never written, yet the function returns 0 (success) at line 23 — presenting an incomplete operation as successful and leaving uninitialized bytes in the output buffer.

assumptions: cipher and its ->opaque field are produced by qcrypto_cipher_new (not shown); assumed to be a valid QCryptoCipherNettle — cannot serve as trigger or guard.

ctx->alg_decrypt, ctx->niv, ctx->iv, ctx->ctx_decrypt/ctx->ctx_encrypt are set by the cipher-creation code, which is not shown; their values cannot be relied on as guards, and for the supported algorithms niv matches the algorithm block size.
The sizes of the 'in'/'out' buffers are not passed into this function, so no local len-vs-buffer bound is possible; the len <= buffer-size relationship remains an unquotable caller contract.
limitations: A memory-corruption (out-of-bounds write) primitive is not simulated: under nettle's documented semantics a misaligned length aborts (CBC) or silently truncates (ECB) rather than overflowing; the realized impact is a guest-triggerable crash of the higher-privileged QEMU host process (DoS).

The information-disclosure variant (uninitialized trailing bytes of 'out' on the ECB path flowing to a consumer) requires the unshown block-layer consumer of 'out'; that link is outside this code, so it is noted, not counted as the primary impact.
Dereference of 'cipher'/'cipher->opaque' at line 7 without a NULL check requires a caller violating the internal object-creation contract; not instantiated.
The error message at lines 19-20 cites cipher->alg although the failure concerns cipher->mode — cosmetic message misattribution; the branch still fails closed with return -1.

verdict.summary: flashsv2_prime consumes the attacker-supplied prime pointer src and byte count size with no local validation: src is bound to s->zstream.next_in and size to s->zstream.avail_in and immediately passed to inflate() without any NULL, range, or sign check on any path. A caller-supplied NULL src is dereferenced inside inflate(), and a negative size widens to a huge unsigned avail_in causing an out-of-bounds read past the source buffer, crashing the process that decodes the attacker-crafted FlashSV v2 stream (denial of service). The single missing guard is the entry check (upstream added: if (!src || !size) return AVERROR(EINVAL);).

evidence.reason: Root cause: the intake parameters src and size are bound directly into the zlib stream and consumed by inflate() at line 12 with no preceding validation (no NULL check, no range/sign check, no clamp anywhere in the function; the only error arms at lines 13 and 21 guard unrelated operations and run after first use). Instantiated trigger: src = NULL with size > 0 causes a NULL pointer dereference inside inflate; size < 0 converts to a huge uInt avail_in causing an out-of-bounds read past the source buffer. Either crashes the decoder process on attacker-supplied media (DoS).

assumptions: The caller of this static helper (the FlashSV v2 prime path passing packet/extradata bytes) is not shown; per the width-domain rule src and size are treated as attacker-data instantiable at any value of their declared types, including NULL src and negative size.

s->block_size, s->deflate_block_size, s->tmpblock, s->deflate_block are set by code not shown; this function relies on unquoted contracts that tmpblock is at least block_size*3 bytes and deflate_block at least deflate_block_size bytes, both non-negative.
On zlib versions hardened against NULL next_in (>= 1.2.12), the NULL-src path degrades to an ignored Z_STREAM_ERROR; the negative-size path still yields a huge avail_in read bound on those versions.
limitations: size == 0 alone is benign: simulation shows inflate makes no progress, the deflate sync round-trip moves at most 4 bytes, and the function returns 0; the !size half of the upstream guard is defensive rather than crash-fixing.

A negative or overflowing s->block_size / s->deflate_block_size (e.g. block_size making block_size*3 overflow int, or a negative field widening to a huge uInt avail_out at lines 11/18/28) could cause a heap out-of-bounds write via inflate/deflate, but the overflow depends on the actual allocation sizes of tmpblock/deflate_block, which are not shown and not derivable from this code, so this candidate is speculative.

Unchecked inflate()/deflate() return values have no memory-safety consequence since zlib bounds all writes by avail_out; the defect there is correctness-only (a corrupt prime payload silently primes a garbage dictionary and still returns 0).
Whether OOB-read bytes (negative-size path) could reach decoded output frames is not shown; the asserted impact is the cross-boundary crash/DoS itself.

verdict.summary: dprintf_formatf writes attacker-controlled precision digits backward from workend into the fixed-size stack buffer work[] without any upper bound on prec (lines 205-209), enabling an attacker-length-controlled out-of-bounds stack write (e.g. curl_mprintf("%.*d", 100000, 42)); independently, in the FORMAT_DOUBLE case the precision clamp (lines 376-377) only reserves space for the %f shape (integer digits + '.'), not for the %e/%g exponent or sign characters, so (sprintf)(work, formatbuf, p->data.dnum) at line 396 overflows work[] (e.g. "%.125e" of 5.0 writes 132 bytes).

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds stack write (CWE-787). prec is attacker-controlled (from an argument via line 119 or from format-string digits via line 128) and is never upper-bounded anywhere on the FORMAT_INT/FORMAT_PTR path; w starts at workend = &work[sizeof(work)-2] (line 32/192) and decrements once per iteration, so any prec >= BUFFSIZE writes '0' bytes below work[0]. Simulated trigger: precision argument 100000 with "%.*d" of 42 yields ~99998 backward writes, ~99875 bytes past the buffer start — attacker-controlled-length stack corruption.

Taint origin for candidate A: the field precision is taken directly from a variadic argument ("%.*"-style specs) whose full long domain is instantiable; the only subsequent handling, if(prec < 0) prec = -1 (lines 122-125), addresses negatives only.

Buffer overflow through the classic dangerous function sprintf (CWE-120). formatbuf is assembled from attacker-controlled width/precision and flags; the only clamps — if(width >= (long)sizeof(work)) width = sizeof(work)-1 (lines 359-360) and if(prec > (long)maxprec) prec = maxprec-1 (lines 376-377) — reserve only the %f-shaped output (integer digits plus '.'), never the %e/%g exponent ('e+00'.. up to 5 chars) or the sign/'#' flag characters. Simulated trigger: "%.125e" with dnum 5.0 passes the clamp unmodified (125 > 126 is false) and sprintf writes "5." + 125 '0's + "e+00" = 132 bytes into work[BUFFSIZE] (128), overflowing the stack buffer by at least 4 bytes for any BUFFSIZE.

Root cause of the line-396 overflow: this is the only precision bound on the FORMAT_DOUBLE path, and it is structurally insufficient — maxprec = sizeof(work)-2 minus integer-part digits accounts only for a fixed-point layout, allows prec == maxprec at the boundary, and ignores the exponent/sign/appended characters, so it cannot keep the sprintf output inside work[].

assumptions: BUFFSIZE, MAX_PARAMETERS, lower_digits/upper_digits, OUTCHAR, va_stack_t, dprintf_Pass1, dprintf_DollarString, and curl_msnprintf are defined outside the given code; BUFFSIZE is 128 in upstream curl, but candidate A is independent of its value (any precision >= BUFFSIZE overflows), and candidate B's overflow (min output B+5 bytes into work[B]) is structural for any BUFFSIZE.

dprintf_Pass1 is assumed to parse the format per standard printf semantics (registering precision parameters and FLAGS_PREC/FLAGS_PRECPARAM) as its call-site comments describe; without this no %-spec reaches the switch at all.
OUTCHAR is assumed to stream characters through the stream() callback rather than buffer into work[].
limitations: p = &vto[param] (line 99) indexes vto with param from dprintf_DollarString with no local check against MAX_PARAMETERS; an out-of-range "%<large>$" would give an OOB p whose p->flags/p->type are read and whose p->data.ptr is written in FORMAT_INTPTR (line 415). Not promoted to primary because reachability of an out-of-range positional spec past the quoted gate if(dprintf_Pass1(format, vto, endpos, ap_save)) return -1; (lines 35-36) cannot be determined from the shown code — Pass1's acceptance criteria are not quotable.

maxprec-- (lines 371-374) underflows size_t when the double's integer part has more than sizeof(work)-2 digits (val >= 1e126 for BUFFSIZE 128); the resulting negative prec produces a malformed ".-175e"-style conversion spec passed to sprintf, whose behavior is undefined but which does not instantiate a demonstrated overflow.
left is not decremented after the precision is appended to formatbuf (line 380); computed worst-case fptr usage (~16 bytes of the 32-byte formatbuf) means formatbuf itself does not overflow.
f = *end++ (line 423) relies on endpos[] entries created by the unshown dprintf_Pass1; a mismatch would dereference an uninitialized/NULL entry, but this depends entirely on unshown code.
width -= prec (line 206) can underflow the long width, but width only feeds OUTCHAR streaming loops (no memory sink), matching ordinary printf semantics; not counted as a vulnerability.

verdict.summary: flashsv2_prime sizes zlib memory operations directly from unvalidated attacker-influenced values: it sets the inflate write bound from `s->block_size * 3` (a FlashSV2 context field whose producer/allocation basis is not shown, with no local range, overflow, or capacity check) and the read bound from the unchecked `int size` parameter. An out-of-range block_size (negative, or > INT_MAX/3 so the product wraps, or exceeding the tmpblock allocation basis) converts to a huge unsigned avail_out, and `inflate(&s->zstream, Z_SYNC_FLUSH)` then writes decompressed data past s->tmpblock — a heap out-of-bounds write triggered by a crafted Flash Screen Video v2 file. The only checks in the function (`if (!src)`, deflateInit, inflateReset) guard none of these values.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds write. avail_out is the memory-write bound zlib inflate uses when writing decompressed data into s->tmpblock; it is computed from s->block_size, an attacker-influenced context field (set from FlashSV2 frame data by code not shown) with no local validation: no non-negativity check, no overflow check on the `* 3` (block_size > INT_MAX/3 wraps negative), no capacity check against tmpblock. The mention sweep (lines 13, 18, 30) shows no guard anywhere. With block_size out of range (e.g. 0x40000000 gives avail_out = 3221225472 after signed-overflow wrap and unsigned conversion), inflate writes past tmpblock — heap buffer overflow caused by a crafted file.

Second occurrence of the same unguarded sink: the same unvalidated `s->block_size * 3` is used as the write bound for a second inflate into s->tmpblock, giving a second attacker-triggered heap out-of-bounds write on the same path (no intervening check on block_size exists between lines 13 and 30).

Out-of-bounds read (same missing-validation class, read side). size is an int parameter whose producer is not shown and which is never checked in this function; a negative size converts to a huge unsigned avail_in, and the inflate call at line 14 then reads past the end of the src packet buffer. The only mention of size is this line; no guard exists on any path.

assumptions: FlashSVContext struct declaration, the allocation sites and producers of s->block_size, s->deflate_block_size, s->tmpblock, s->deflate_block, and the inflateInit of s->zstream are outside the shown code; per the width-domain rule their values are treated as full-domain attacker data, and per guard-anchoring their external consistency may not serve as a guard.

zlib avail_in/avail_out are unsigned (uInt), so negative int assignments convert to values near 4 billion; inflate/deflate read at most avail_in bytes from next_in and write at most avail_out bytes to next_out (standard zlib semantics).
src and size originate from the demuxed packet, i.e., the parsed FlashSV file — a trust-boundary payload.
limitations: The exact out-of-bounds extent depends on tmpblock's actual allocated size, which is not shown; the overflow itself is independent of that size because the write bound is derived without any comparison to it.

The unchecked return values of inflate() (lines 14, 31) and deflate() (line 21) have no memory-safety consequence inside this function (avail_out is only decreased by zlib, keeping line 18's subtraction consistent, and inflateReset is checked before reuse) — robustness only, not counted as a vulnerability.

If a negative size is deemed unreachable because the unshown caller computes it from non-negative packet offsets, candidate A (line 11) would be speculative; the primary verdict rests on the block_size write bound (lines 13-14, 30-31), which does not depend on that assumption.

verdict.verdict_message: No memory-safety vulnerability found: all attacker-reachable sinks are protected by quoted, correctly ordered, correctly bounded guards.
verdict.summary: Server-side VNC extended-clipboard parser. All attacker-controlled values (message length, flags, per-format lengths) reaching memory sinks are guarded by quoted checks in correct execution order: 'if (len < 4) throw' before 'len - 4'; 'if (len > maxCutText) { is->skip(len); return; }' bounding processed size; 'if (len < (rdr::S32)(4 + 4*num)) throw' before the caps length reads; and 'if (lengths[num] > (size_t)maxCutText) { ... continue; }' placed before 'new rdr::U8[lengths[num]]' and 'zis.readBytes(buffers[num], lengths[num])', with the allocation sized from the same expression as the copy length. The reject path ('flags &= ~(1 << i); continue;' without num++) keeps the delete loop exactly consistent with the allocation loop, so no uninitialized delete, double free, or leak occurs on in-code paths. Remaining candidates (unbounded caps lengths passed to handleClipboardCaps, buffer leak if a ZlibInStream call throws, decompression amplification via zis.skip of values up to 0xFFFFFFFF) all depend on unshown internal callees whose behavior cannot instantiate a trigger or impact under the analysis rules; they are recorded as limitations.

assumptions: maxCutText is an operator-configured global (producer not shown) assumed non-negative; a negative value would make the (size_t)maxCutText guard vacuous, but it is not attacker-settable and would still not create an overflow because allocation and copy use the identical length expression.

ZlibInStream (zis) and the handler->handleClipboard* callbacks are project-internal and not shown; per the analysis rules their behavior is an assumption that can neither produce a trigger nor guard a sink.

clipboardActionMask / clipboardCaps / clipboardProvide / clipboardRequest / clipboardPeek / clipboardNotify are compile-time constants not shown; the switch is fully enumerated with a default arm that throws.
limitations: Caps branch: the U32 lengths read at 'lengths[num++] = is->readU32();' are never validated against any bound (unlike the provide branch) and are passed raw to handler->handleClipboardCaps(flags, lengths). If the unshown handler used them as allocation sizes or indices, that would be a downstream defect; in this code the call is a capability-recording callback, not a memory/copy/indexing operation, so the impact chain is not instantiated here.

No exception safety around the provide loop: if any zis.readU32()/zis.skip()/zis.readBytes() call throws (e.g., on truncated compressed data) after one or more 'new rdr::U8[...]' allocations, the delete loop at the end is never reached and up to 15*maxCutText bytes leak per message; repeatable across messages as a potential memory-exhaustion DoS. The throw itself depends on the unshown ZlibInStream's overrun behavior, so the trigger is not instantiable from the given code.

zis.skip(lengths[num]) is called with values up to 0xFFFFFFFF (the rejected 'too long' path), forcing decompression of the entire remaining message payload; zlib's maximum expansion ratio (~1000:1) gives a repeatable per-message CPU/memory amplification bounded only by maxCutText compressed bytes per message. Design-inherent decompression-bomb concern, not a memory-safety defect in this code.

is->skip(len) with attacker-stated len up to INT32_MAX (line 10) consumes that many bytes from the socket; if the client withholds them, only that connection's reader thread stalls — per-connection DoS at most, no memory corruption.

verdict.summary: read_sm_data parses attacker-controlled media stream data. In the CodecSpecificSide branch, value_len (int64_t from ffio_read_varlen) is validated only against an upper bound (`avio_tell(bc) + value_len >= maxpos`), so a negative value_len passes. The side-data allocation size `value_len + 8` is then implicitly truncated to int and can be as small as 1, while AV_WB64 unconditionally writes 8 bytes to that buffer, producing a heap out-of-bounds write with attacker-controlled content when a malicious file supplies name='CodecSpecificSide<digits>' and a negative/varlen-wrapped value_len.

evidence.reason: Heap out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). The allocation size is the int-truncated value of the attacker-controlled int64 value_len + 8, which can be 1..7 when value_len's low 32 bits are 0xFFFFFFF9..0xFFFFFFFF, while AV_WB64(dst, v64) always writes 8 bytes. The `if(!dst)` check only rejects a NULL allocation, not an undersized one. Trigger: file supplies name matching 'CodecSpecificSide%d' and a varlen encoding value_len = -7; the only bound check (line 31) passes because avio_tell(bc) + negative value_len < maxpos, so 8 attacker-influenced bytes are written into a 1-byte heap side-data buffer.

Origin and inadequate guard of the tainted value. value_len is a fully attacker-controlled int64_t read from the media stream (full int64 domain per its declared width), but the only check is a one-sided upper bound: negative value_len values make avio_tell(bc) + value_len negative and pass the `>= maxpos` test, so no statement rejects value_len < 0 anywhere in the function.

assumptions: maxpos is supplied by the demuxer (not shown) and treated as internal-trusted; the instantiated trigger (negative value_len) passes the line-31 check for any maxpos greater than the current stream position.

ffio_read_varlen accumulates attacker stream bytes into a uint64 without a byte-count cap in this code; regardless, value_len's declared int64_t width makes the negative domain instantiable per the width-domain rule.
av_packet_new_side_data(size) is documented to allocate exactly `size` bytes and return NULL for size <= 0; internal padding inside that callee is not a quotable guard in this code.
limitations: Unchecked get_str return values at lines 24 and 29: str_value/type_str are passed to av_log without a sentinel check, a defect at the use site, but the concrete impact (uninitialized or non-NUL-terminated buffer reaching the log) depends on the unshown failure semantics of get_str, so it was not counted as a primary finding.

A huge `count` (up to INT_MAX) combined with an exhausted stream could cause many iterations if get_str consumes no bytes at EOF; termination depends on unshown get_s/get_str EOF behavior, so this is a potential unbounded-consumption concern, not confirmed here.
avio_skip(bc, value_len) with negative value_len (line 48) seeks backward in the stream; no memory-safety effect was found in this code from that path.

verdict.summary: In _php_mb_regex_ereg_replace_exec, when a pattern matches with zero width at the end of the subject string, the match-advance path executes `pos++` with no upper-bound check against string_lim, so pos becomes str.data() + str.size() + 1. The next loop iteration passes this out-of-domain pointer as the `start` argument to onig_search, causing the regex engine to scan/read past the end of the subject buffer (out-of-bounds read); if a match over the out-of-range position is reported, `out_buf.append((const char *)pos, (OnigUChar *)(str.data() + regs->beg[0]) - pos)` receives a negative length converted to a huge unsigned size. Trigger is fully attacker-instantiated (e.g., pattern "x*", subject "abc", any replacement). The only nearby bound, `if (pos < string_lim)`, guards just the 1-byte append, not the increment, and the empty-match rejection that would block it is compiled out under `#if moriyoshi_0`.

evidence.reason: Root cause: `pos++` is executed without any check that pos < string_lim. When an empty-width match occurs at the end of the subject (e.g., pattern "x*" with subject "abc"), the iteration that matches at pos == string_lim takes this else branch, skips the guarded append, and increments pos to string_lim + 1 — one byte beyond the buffer extent. The `if (pos < string_lim)` check guards only the append on the previous line, not the increment.

Sink: on the loop iteration following the overflow, pos == str.data() + str.size() + 1 is passed as the `start` argument while `end` and `range` are str.data() + str.size(), i.e., start is outside the search domain [str, end]. No statement on any path validates pos against string_lim before this call, so the regex engine is invoked on a pointer past the end of the buffer, producing an out-of-bounds read; if it reports a match with beg[0] <= str.size(), the append at lines 80-81 then computes a negative length that converts to a near-SIZE_MAX unsigned copy size.

assumptions: Oniguruma documented semantics for in-domain calls: a successful onig_search returns match offsets within [0, str.size()] with num_regs >= 1 for group 0, and an OnigRegion is reusable after onig_region_free(region, 0) — these protect the backreference append (lines 93-98) and the pre-match append (lines 80-81) for in-domain pos.
php_mb_mbchar_bytes_ex is assumed (internal callee, not shown) to return a character length >= 1; the copy at line 102 is bounded by `remaining >= fwd` for any returned value.
_php_mb_regex_init_options and php_mbregex_compile_pattern are internal callees not shown; their results (options, syntax, re) are either NULL-checked (re) or only affect regex semantics.
limitations: regs = onig_region_new() (line 62) is not NULL-checked; on allocation failure, `regs->num_regs` (line 93) would be a NULL dereference. Only triggerable by memory exhaustion, not by attacker input — robustness issue, not counted.

If php_mb_mbchar_bytes_ex could return 0 for some lead byte, lines 101-104 would loop forever appending zero bytes (CPU denial of service); this depends on an unshown internal callee and could not be instantiated from the given code.

The concrete out-of-bounds read occurs inside Oniguruma once the out-of-domain start pointer is passed; if the linked Oniguruma version rejects start > end with an error code, the code path degrades to a 'mbregex search failure' warning and an incorrect return instead of memory unsafety. Per the call-site rule (discipline 3), passing the unvalidated out-of-range pointer is counted as the defect in this code; confidence reflects that the memory-unsafe realization depends on callee behavior not shown.
